speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, January 31, 1983, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde that Bill C-139, to amend the statute law relating to income tax (No. 2), be read the second time and referred to a Committee of the Whole.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO STATUTE LAW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House rose on the last occasion when this Bill was under discussion, I was detailing for the House the various meetings which have been held by the Progressive Conservative Party to examine in detail the original budget brought in by the late Finance Minister of the Liberal Party. I had gone through that at length. Today I want to mention some of the specific items which we were able to persuade the Government to withdraw, and then I will deal with some remaining matters concerning Bill C-139.
As a result of the efforts of the Progressive Conservative Party, the Government has withdrawn its ill-fated plan to tax employee health and dental benefits. It has delayed the implementation of the shift of manufacturers' sales tax to the wholesale level until mid-1984. It has changed the rules with regard to the small business dividend distribution tax, and that will apply only to dividends paid out of incomes earned in the taxation years starting after 1982. It has withdrawn the proposal that interest on money borrowed to earn investment income be deducted only against investment income. The automobile standby tax has been reduced from 2.5 per cent to 2 per cent. It has made significant changes in its proposal to tax whole life insurance policies and has made several improvements.
Today I want to discuss the items which have been left in, specifically with respect to employees, small businesses and farmers. The Liberal Government originally planned to sock it to all employees. For years, we on this side of the House have been encouraging unions to bargain for health and dental insurance. To our Party, it made good sense for us as a country to support the healthy Canadian family. In the original budget, the Liberal Party attacked the basic principle that families should look after themselves and decided it would tax employee health and dental plans. Now that proposal has been
withdrawn, but I want to deal at length with one item which has been left in concerning the question of mobility.
Canada is a large country, and we must encourage mobility in our economic thinking. Companies have traditionally offered interest subsidies to employees moving from one part of Canada to another where there is a housing shortage and high prices, thus costing the employee more to remain at the same housing level. In November the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) proposed to tax all interest subsidies, effective 1982. In December, 1981 that exemption was withdrawn over two years for loans that were already in effect. In June, 1982 the Government decided it would not apply to commitments made prior to the budget.
[DOT] (mo)
I am pointing out these various "back and forths" to point out to the House that the Government does not really understand the problem. It does not understand why housing loans are made. It does not recognize the need for the Government to assist Canadians to be as mobile as possible in finding jobs in these days of high unemployment.
The second reason I am pointing these out is the absolute inability of the Government to understand that you have to phase in tax changes. Tax changes cannot be made overnight. It is one thing to say that it is the intention of the Government to tax loans on housing and that that is going to be phased in. To phase these changes in overnight is something else again. That is what our party is objecting to, the immediate change in taxation policy, which means that the businesses and employees who have arranged their affairs suddenly find that the Government has changed the rules of the game.
One of the most petty rules of the Liberal Government in the 1981 budget was the decision to increase sharply the taxation of employer-owned or leased automobiles which are used by salespeople. Bill C-139 now proposes to charge employees a stand-by fee equal to 2 per cent per month of the purchase price of the automobile if the employer owns the automobile and two-thirds of the lease costs if the car is leased. In simple terms, what the Liberals are saying is that if an employee uses a leased vehicle, he or she is using that car for eight months for his or her personal purposes and for four months for the purpose of earning income, and that simply does not make sense.
There have been other things which we do not agree with in terms of employee benefits, but I want to deal with small business. Small business, as the House well knows, is the backbone of the Canadian economy and this Bill is a direct attack by the Government on the small business community.

February 7, 1983
Income Tax
Small business was traditionally encouraged to invest in capital assets by the fact that a full year's depreciation or capital cost allowance could be taken in the year of purchase. Now the Government has changed all that. It is now saying that an asset purchased in the first month of the business year will be eligible for the same depreciation as assets purchased in the twelfth month of the first year.
My question to the Members on the Government side is, would it not make more sense to allow capital cost allowance to be calculated according to the month of purchase in the first year? Therefore, if the purchase was made in the first month of the business year, they could claim twelve months' depreciation. If they purchase it in the fifth month, they could claim seven months' depreciation.
This is the time for some innovative thinking on the part of the Government, not for thinking which discourages capital investment. If capital cost allowance is cut in the first year, that discourages capital investment. The reason we have so much shut-down in our manufacturing industry is because of that one provision.
The next point I would like to speak on is the Small Business Development Bond, which was originally introduced by the Progressive Conservative Government in December, 1979 to help small businesses weather the ravages of high interest rates. This was a consolidating feature which allowed small businesses to consolidate their debts on a once in a lifetime basis. There was strong support for that concept in the business community.
In April, 1980 we retained the name but changed the philosophy. In order to qualify, a small business had to be expanding. In times of economic problems, the Government wanted them to expand. Then we had the final insult. In November, 1981, to get a Small Business Development Bond a business had to be going broke. That does not make any sense at all. This Government rewards killers, spies and businesses going broke. It just does not make any sense.
[DOT] (U15)

speechtext:
The Hon. Member's viewpoint has always been well respected by himself.
I want to talk about interest deductibility. If Canada is going to grow, we have to encourage Canadians to invest in Canada. In November, 1981 the Liberals proposed to eliminate the interest expense deduction if it exceeded interest income. What the Liberals did not realize was that it occasionally takes time for investment income to exceed investment expense.
It is easy to understand the confusion. After all, Arthur Erickson did not have to wait for his investment in the Liberal Party to pay dividends. Ian Sinclair has not had to wait. He signed on the blue ribbon committee in the summer and he got Bill S-31. If that was not enough, he got the changes in the Crow rate which are going to benefit only the railways. Therefore, it is easy to understand the thinking of the heavyduty supporters of the Liberal Government. They want their investment return right away. However, they suggest that the ordinary Canadian investor has to wait. Fortunately, after we explained the facts of life to the bureaucrats, they backed down.
The last group I want to deal with in speaking to Bill C-139 is the farmers. The Liberal Party and its bureaucrats simply do not understand that the family farm is the Canadian farmer's pension plan. My constituents work hard on a day-to-day basis to put something aside for retirement. That retirement plan, shall we call it, consists of paying off the family farm.
The Hon. Member laughs. I would not laugh about that. I appreciate that the Hon. Member comes from a metropolitan riding, but I would not laugh about the plight of the Canadian farmer. I do not think that is fair for a metropolitan Toronto Member to do.
That retirement nest-egg is created by paying off the family farm. What the farmer does is sell the farm and take back a mortgage. Before the Government changed the rules, a farmer could sell his farm and invest the capital gain portion in an income-averaging annuity. That allowed him to plan for retirement. He could calculate his chances for surviving and for how long, invest the money and get an annuity. The Liberals have changed all that. Just as the laughter on the other side has demonstrated, how many Liberals and bureaucrats own farms? They do not have any idea of what is happening out there, no idea whatsoever. Instead of the incomeaveraging annuity content, the farmers of Canada will now be faced with the uncertainty of general averaging.
I want to sum up now because I have had two chances to speak to this Bill. I urge the Government to bring forward Bill C-139 on a serious basis. This is the third day of debate, but in fact we only had one full day of debate before this. The second day was interrupted by a debate on Standing Order 81, plus, if you can believe it, Royal Assent in the middle of the debate on Bill C-139.
We on this side of the House urge the Government to give some certainty and finality to income tax legislation in this country by bringing forward Bill C-139 on a chunk basis so that we can have all the debate at one time and Members in every part of the House can be heard. That will bring some certainty into the lives of accountants, lawyers, small business people, farmers and employees in this country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to compliment the Hon. Member for an interesting and partisan speech. He presented his point of view from a very clear bias. I would like to explore one or two of those nuances.
The Hon. Member said that mobility among Canadian workers must be encouraged and that the question of home
February 7, 1983

loans from employers being viewed as a taxable benefit discourages this kind of mobility. I believe he said that. Taking the hypothetical case of two people working for the Ford Motor Company, one an executive and one working on the assembly line, if both of them have to move from Windsor to Oakville, it has been the practice of such companies to subsidize the mortgages of the executives but not of the workers on the assembly line. Therefore, these workers not only go without the tax-free benefit, but they help to pay for the other man's tax-free benefit. Could the Flon. Member give us some idea of how fair he thinks that kind of equation is?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO STATUTE LAW
speechtext:
I should start out by saying that I appreciate the Hon. Member's compliment on my speech. I must say I have no hesitancy in speaking from a biased viewpoint in favour of small business, farmers and employees.
To answer the question directly, 1 would say the Hon. Members is correct. In my opinion, which I believe would be shared by my Party, if there are going to be loans for employees who are moved by their company, it seems to me eminently fair that the loan should be for all levels of employment. We in this Party, to the best of my knowledge, make no distinction between the executive and the highly skilled worker. If Ford Motor Company, or any company, is going to make loans to enable people to transfer their place of employment without suffering, then as far as we are concerned the executive and the highly skilled worker on the assembly line should get the same break. There is absolutely no question of that. As a matter of fact, if that is happening I would hope the Government is clamping down on it.
The point remains, however, that we want to move people across this country. We want to encourage that. Mobility is referred to in the Charter of Rights, and what that means is that we want companies to flourish in Canada, including Calgary and Vancouver where house prices are out of sight. If a company has to loan a highly skilled worker or an executive money to purchase a house, perhaps there should be some clause in the contract that if there is a capital gain realized, the company would receive a piece of it. We should treat all employees equally and encourage mobility.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO STATUTE LAW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to see the Hon. Member wants everyone treated equally. 1 agree with that perspective. I would like to point out to him that there are instances in my riding where whole companies have moved and everyone, from the president to the janitor, is offered a home subsidy. That is interesting but it is the exception, not the rule. What I have described to the Hon. Member is more common, that someone working on an assembly line cannot get that kind of subsidy.
I wonder if the Hon. Member could pursue his point one step further and describe how someone moving on his own hook, as is common, from Newfoundland to the oil fields in Alberta, could get this kind of a tax break. An employee can get it, but someone moving on his own hook cannot. What is the fairness in that?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think that the best I could do for the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fisher) is to suggest to him that those provisions are in the Act already. If he takes a hard look at them, he will find there are provisions for deduction of moving expenses. I do not have the same familiarity with the Act that 1 had, but 1 would be willing to take that up with the Parliamentary Secretary later.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO STATUTE LAW
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to pursue that point of the question even further. With regard to moving expenses, the Hon. Member is correct. Would he also indicate the fairness of the situation where an individual moves from Calgary, say, to Ottawa, buys a house, takes up employment, and does not receive any consideration, with respect to moving, of a mortgage loan which is tax deductible or tax free, whereas someone from Ottawa calls someone in Calgary, offers them a job and gives them an interest-free loan for the house they purchase in Ottawa? The two individuals are in exactly the same situation, but one has a tax-free or very low-interest loan to purchase a house and the other one has not. Can the Hon. Member comment on the fairness of that situation?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO STATUTE LAW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the Hon. Member's confirmation that in the Act there was a deduction for moving expenses for people moving on their own. I can understand that there is a problem. Naturally, under the mortgage interest and realty tax deduction plan that the Progressive Conservative Party had in place the individual who had to take up a mortgage to move to Ottawa would be looked after and would be able to deduct those expenses from income. That provision is already in our Party's platform.
However, I think the Hon. Member will find, as the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance suggested, that different companies have different policies. What we were dealing with was this. 1 think within the free enterprise system it is equitable for company "A", which manufactures widgets, to have a different system from company "B" which also manufactures widgets, because if company "A" have that plan, they would probably be better able to encourage good employees to come to work for them. That is the situation within the free enterprise system.
As I suggested, the plan should be applied across the board. It should apply to executives and highly skilled workers, anyone who works for the company; no question about that. If the company has to move its janitor to Calgary, the janitor should get the same break as the vice-president. I have no hesitation in saying that at all.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to participate in the debate on Bill C-139. I was not really too surprised to find the Progressive Conservative Party, through their spokesman today, the Hon. Member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis), taking credit for all the changes made in the November, 1981 budget. I think he probably had his tongue firmly planted in his cheek when he made that kind of representation, knowing that back-benchers

February 7, 1983
Income Tax
on this side had a fair amount to do with many of the changes which have taken place, many of them for the better. Not only do we take full credit for that, but we are prepared to share that credit with the business community and labour groups which came forward and spoke to the Minister and the Department of Finance and indicated where there were some burrs in this particular budget which had to be removed if it was going to be equitable and applicable to the whole of the country.
This Bill now represents the culmination of a great deal of work and debate, and some change. With a budget in 1981 and later financial statements, the Government could hardly be seen to be ramming this Bill through the House. It can be called new or recent because it was tabled early in December, but the contents have been comprehensibly scrutinized by the public, Opposition and Government Members, and by and large by the business community and labour groups throughout the country. So it has had a good debate. We also know that the subject matter of the Bill was referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, and representations came from that particular Committee, many of which are found in Bill C-139. So the Bill has been, I think, long, effectively and comprehensibly debated.
The problem which flows, I think, was highlighted in part by the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) in his address on this particular part of the Bill; that is, Mr. Speaker, the process. It is no secret that anyone involved at any time with the preparing of a budget would not agree with the present method of doing so. We have yet to find a perfect method, but I think we have to keep searching to see if there is not some better way so that the kind of certainty that the Hon. Member for Simcoe North was talking about will be known to the general public and it will not require a year or a year and a half of debate before items recommended or suggested in a budget see the light of day.
Unfortunately, people who have tried that in the East have almost been hoist with their own petard. When the Hon. Walter Gordon was Minister of Finance, he thought it would be good procedure to bring in people from the business community to let them see what the bureaucrats, the Departments and the Minister were proposing and find out whether they could propose a counterbalance or some improvements on the suggestions being made. 1 thought that was a great pioneering move but, unhappily, attention was focused on the three individuals brought in from the business community. There were questions about whether they were on a leave of absence, whether certain benefits were accruing to them or to their firms as a result of advising the Minister, and not enough attention was focused on the positive, courageous step taken by the Hon. Walter Gordon in trying to improve the process.
Next came the white paper method. That offered an opportunity to muse in public about how the next budget might be put together, the sort of things that should be contained in it and the ramifications if certain steps were taken. Unfortunately, it was not regarded as a white paper but as Government
policy. The Government found itself having to defend everything in the white paper as if it were Government policy instead of a proposition offered in the hope that the Canadian public would see the things that might be possible and also see the problems that face a Government endeavouring to prepare a budget that was equitable. There was reaction against the white paper and considerable attention paid to the more reprehensible parts of it, rather than concentration on the positive aspects. As a result, that process did not see the light of day.
I served as Parliamentary Secretary to a Minister of Finance who did not particularly care for the secrecy that was involved in the budget. He felt that it was something that we inherited, but that has long since been abandoned in the Westminster system where there is more consultation with the general public. After seeing the disaster of the white paper, he decided to consult with colleagues that he trusted, Ministers who had the same responsibility to their Provinces as he had to Canada, namely, to put a budget together. They bounced ideas off each other, trying to find out what the implications of certain moves would be for Ontario, say, Quebec or for the Atlantic provinces-whether a certain action would be the correct use of tax points and so on.
All in all, people in the political arena-and 1 emphasize people in the political arena-with some knowledge of budgets, some knowledge of the process and of the impact, were able to come up with what was, 1 think, a budget good enough to be defeated in the House and, subsequently, for the Liberal Party to win an election on. It was a better budget as a result of that consultation than it would have been without.
The Hon. Member for Simcoe North claimed that the Government is prepared to rush this Bill through but he ignored the debate that has been going on since November, 1981. The Bill before us is the culmination of the many, many representations that have been made. What we have here is a study in semantics. I think the changes that have been made are appropriate, that the Bill is better because of them and the budget was better because of them. The Opposition sees this as backing down and, of course, Members of the Government, with their own particular bias, see it as the Government being more flexible. Personally, I think further changes could be made, but this is a necessary element of the present process. Until the night that the budget is read in the House we do not know what it will contain. By its very nature it demands that debate and consultation take place after the fact.
How much better it would be if we could come up with a process to do that before the fact. Some areas could be kept secret because of the stock market or because someone might have inside information. We should question certain approaches, such as indexing-whether it is worth keeping or worth the cost of $7 billion or $8 billion of Government revenues. Such things could be the subject of legitimate debate. This is not the case at the present time, because if an item is not on the bill, it cannot be discussed. All we can do is guess at the subjects the budget will cover. We debate what
February 7, 1983

might be in the budget, only to find that it is not there and all that debate is wasted.
I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) is embarking on an excellent process of consultation in moving this Bill before the Finance Committee so that there can be better debate. 1 hope he will not be rushed into bringing down his next budget, however, but that he will take time to consult again with groups in order to ensure that the actions he is contemplating will not have severe and negative implications for the business community.
When the Minister spoke to representatives of business in late January, he said:
We must build the foundation for a tougher, more productive, more competitive economy. And we must do it while combatting the painful effects of a world recession that has hit Canada harder precisely because of our greater dependence on world trade.
He is saying to the business community, to workers and to the public generally, that we have to become lean and mean if we are to succeed in the post-recession market.
It has been difficult for the Government, also for the Conservatives who were once in Government, to put to rest the belief that simple solutions are possible to our economic problems, and most notably the belief that Government can do it all and can end our economic problems. The general public is much more knowledgeable today and recognizes that whether the Government works in concert with the Provinces or whether the Provinces work in concert with the municipalities, no Government can go it alone. It needs the help of the general public.
What can be done to help, Mr. Speaker? Legislators can help bring in the best possible legislation and the public has an obligation to become as productive as possible. If there is one area where the country is failing, it is in the area of productivity. I know that my friend, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), will be quick to point out that the Canadian farmer is probably the most productive person in the community. We must improve productivity, however, and that is not to slam labour or management. It is a clarion call to recognize one of our major problems, that we are not as productive as we need to be in order to compete.
As the Minister of Finance has said, no one would be happier than he if it were possible to solve unemployment by forgetting about inflation. That would result in fewer jobs, however, not more. Only a few months ago we had high inflation and high unemployment at the same time. The inflation rate is coming down and we have an obligation, through legislation like this, to see to it that unemployment also comes down. To the extent that the economy cannot absorb all those who want to work at the present time, the Government has an obligation to provide jobs, both short term and long term but more appropriately long term. We cannot ignore that problem. That is why money must be and is being spent to train people for the jobs that will become available so that we may be in the forefront of the economies of the western world.
Income Tax
It is not difficult to approve this Bill in principle, Mr. Speaker. Any piece of legislation can be improved, but at second reading we deal with the principle of the Bill. We will deal with the nitty-gritty when it goes before committee for clause-by-clause study. The package of tax rate cuts, modification of federal tax credits and cutbacks that are proposed will result in over 93 per cent of tax filers either having a reduction in tax or no tax increase. That is a rather phenomenal thing in the present state of the economy.
1 think everyone can support the increase in the Child Tax Credit which is now $343, an increase of about $50. It could be argued that it should be more and, of course, it would be great if we could provide more. But it is significant that the Government is prepared to make this move at a very difficult time in the economy.
From time to time people will hold up the big Income Tax Act and declare that it is too complex and should be made simpler. We have heard simplistic ideas that if we take 20 per cent of someone's income and pay it to the Government-and the rest is theirs-that will solve all the problems. There is a lot of difference between an individual who earns a $50,000 salary and an individual who earns $50,000 by putting his guts, brains and everything he has-he sacrifices everything- into a small business. The tax Bill is more complicated and complex because we try to build in equities to say to individuals, to entrepreneurs, or to one who is prepared to take a chance, that the Government will back them and give them particular advantages. This is the way complexity is built into the Income Tax Act. It has to be built in in order to make income tax equitable.
There is a tendency from time to time not to go into a sunset situation but to look at some of the incentives which are in place to see whether they should be removed at the present time or whether they should be moved from a particular group and put on to another group because that group is suffering. This could be the case with a businessman, farmer, large corporation or whatever the situation happens to be at the time. We can have a look at it, and if the complexity happens to be there, perhaps we can create equity in other areas by sunsetting some of these situations. I think to be fair that is what was tried in part in November, 1981 without winning too many converts, unhappily. I think in some situations the changes which have been made have been appropriate.
I was pleased to hear the comments of the Hon. Member for Simcoe North. He almost quoted from my speech, judging from what I have written down here. I am sure I heard him say that small business is one of the cornerstones of society. I do not think anyone in the House denies that. They will gain a number of incentives in this particular Bill, signaling the Government's appreciation of the difficult times small-business owners are facing due to world-wide recession. I will cite just a few examples. First, there are the provisions of the Small Business Bond Program, thanks to the Conservatives. They brought them in and we have improved upon and expanded

them. I think it is a better program now than it was at that particular time.

speechtext:
We can have an honest debate between ourselves. I think it is that kind of debate which will make this particular bond even more effective than anything they dream of in their wildest dreams-and they have some dreams on occasion. The program was due to expire at the end of 1982. It reduces interest rates by six to seven percentage points through a tax exemption to lenders. That has now been extended to the end of 1983. The limit on annual income qualifying for low small business tax rate is increased to $200,000 from $150,000. The total accumulated income to qualify goes to $1 million from $750,000. There are items in there, but as I said, we are talking about a Bill at second reading and I do not want to go into the specifics. I am sure they will be dealt with in some detail by the Minister and by members of the committee, whether it be Committee of the Whole or the Bill is ultimately referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
In conclusion, given the present process, which everyone concedes is flawed because of the great insistence upon secrecy, after a Bill is passed-before it is passed, yes, but certainly after it is passed-we have to find out the repercussions of a particular measure in the Bill. We have to be vigilant to the actual benefits which flow. We have to decide whether we can increase the benefits or enhance them, whether the benefits are sufficient so that we can move our emphasis to another area. Also we have to be vigilant to the harmful effects of a piece of legislation and to what extent it deters an individual or detracts from being able to run a better business or being able to take advantage of a tax incentive that will have the effect of increasing the cash flow. We have to watch all these things and see to it when a new budget is drafted and we know the timing of it that we make every effort to bring to the attention of the Department of Finance or the Minister of Finance the areas where we can make changes. Thank heavens we have a budget usually on an annual basis or sometimes twice a year. It gives us an opportunity to make particular changes if they should be made.
The necessity of building as much equity into an income tax Bill, program or budget is absolutely essential in today's day and age. It is a tall order for Government, Parliament or the business community, for that matter, to try to come up with the penultimate answer so that there is equity across the board. The present Income Tax Act goes a long way toward that. It needs a lot of improvement. This particular Bill is an improvement, but I hope we will not be stalled and that we will not hesitate to make recommendations immediately to the Minister of Finance for his next budget. It is a tall order, but it is also our responsibility as those who legislate for the people of Canada.

speechtext: The rules provide at this point for a ten-minute period of questions and answers. Are there any Hon. Members seeking to put questions?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO STATUTE LAW
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was wondering whether the Hon. Member would answer a few questions. He mentioned that small business was important in the development of our economy. Could he find any provisions which specifically help small business? For example, does he consider the half capital cost arrangement to be helpful? Did it inspire people to invest? Did the 12.5 per cent tax on surplus which will be paid out in dividends inspire people to invest? Does the reserve system inspire confidence, where if a man sells his business he has to pay any capital gain within a three-year period? Is that the kind of thing which should be done by a Government that wants to help small business? Could he tell us about anything in the Bill of which he is so proud that helps small businessmen?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO STATUTE LAW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I tried to give some credit where it was due; admittedly, I gave a small amount to the Conservatives for introducing the Small Business Bond. I also pointed out-and I will read it again in case the Hon. Member missed it-that the limit on annual income qualifying for low small business tax rate has been increased to $200,000 from $150,000 and that the total accumulated income to qualify went to $1 million from $750,000.
I would also point out, because this is specifically to what he referred, that the tax rate of 12.5 per cent on dividends paid by small business corporations will apply only to income generated in years commencing after December 31, 1982. This and other changes will significantly simplify the tax, while addressing concerns expressed by small business groups. I gather the Hon. Member was a member of the House of Commons Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. I could deal with almost any piece of legislation and ask, for example, whether the fact that a school teacher has to pay a certain tax encourages him to be a school teacher or to go out and invest.
I could take almost any piece of legislation. The Hon. Member as a counsel knows that. I am sure that in the past he has taken medical reports and ripped them to shreds in court because a client was not hurt as much as he made out. We can all make that kind of attack. But when I talk about helping the future of Canadians, I would like to see something in a more positive vein than simply nitpicking through the Bill.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO STATUTE LAW
speechtext:
I think the Hon. Member will agree that all we have here is a Bill that is not quite as bad as the budget of November. There have been some ameliorations as a result of representations made by this Party, by the public in general and finally by Members on his side of the House to the Minister. Could the Hon. Member advise us as to how the half capital cost allowance arrangement is helping business? How is it inspiring people to invest? Somehow the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Lumley) can say that new capital investment for 1983 is estimated to be down 8 per cent and how reducing capital cost allowances inspired it. subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO STATUTE LAW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on Bill C-139, an Act to amend the statute law relating to income tax. It was given first reading on December 7, 1982. Since the Bill's introduction, I have endeavoured to give it a second reading for my own information and benefit as well as for the information and benefit of the constituents whom I serve in this Parliament. But I say that it has proven to be an almost impossible task.
This Bill contains approximately 295 pages of rules, amendments, double-talk and triple-talk. I submit that no average citizen could understand it. Few Members of Parliament have even read the Bill and even lawyers have difficulty interpreting its complex clauses or stating with certainty the true budget to which these amendments apply.
At present there are four versions of the November, 1981 budget: the version that was introduced; the version as amended on December 18, 1981; the June 28, 1982 version; and the October 27, 1982 version. In addition, there have been minor announcements, and classifications on several occasions, such as a January, 1982 announcement on employee benefits. The fact is that the November budget has been amended so many times that one would literally need a program readily to understand it.
In my opinion, this Bill should not be given speedy passage as requested by Canada's present Finance Minister (Mr. Lalonde). I say this because it is far too lengthy and too far-reaching to be given speedy passage. The Minister stated at a press conference after the Bill received first reading that it is now time to end the uncertainty over our tax laws and let the affected taxpayers know precisely where they stand. He said that quick passage would let the Revenue Department get on with the task of issuing the refunds to which millions of taxpayers will be entitled. He repeated these views during debate in the House on this Bill.
I say that this is nothing more than ministerial nonsense. This Parliament should take its time to make certain that the tax laws it passes are fair and workable. It is not the fault of Members of Parliament or of the Official Opposition that the present Liberal administration brought in a budget that was so unworkable, so unrealistic and unfair, that it took almost 13

February 7, 1983
Income Tax
months of chopping and changing before it could even be properly put before this Parliament. Even if this Bill is passed-and I hope it will be found unacceptable to a majority of Members in the House-Canadian taxpayers will still not know precisely where they stand because the Finance Minister has already indicated that he plans to introduce yet another budget early in 1983.
The charge that any delay will affect taxpayers is ridiculous, since tax returns will not even begin to be processed until some two months from today. Furthermore, the claim that refunds cannot be sent out until this Bill is passed is highly questionable. The Government often applies tax changes almost immediately following a budget night statement by the Minister of Finance. I have seen this happen quite often during my 25-plus years in this Chamber. If taxes can be collected in this manner, I ask why should there be a legal impediment to paying back money to taxpayers from whom it has originally been taken illegally? This Government obviously believes Barnum was right when he said that there is a sucker born every minute.
When the loopholes used mostly by the rich, and which were to be plugged by the November 12 budget, have turned out to be manholes, into which everyone including the Government is falling, then I submit that it becomes necessary for Parliament to take a careful look to ascertain whether our tax system has now become unbalanced by putting an unfair burden on lower income workers.
After reading Bill C-139, I must admit that its contents frighten me. This Bill symbolizes all that is wrong in Canada today. In my estimation, it is a bureaucratic nightmare, for only a bureaucrat, isolated from the cold reality that lies out there, sitting in a warm office here in Ottawa, could come up with this type of legislation which is causing, in effect, 1.6 million Canadians to be unemployed and businessmen from the Atlantic to the Pacific to throw in the towel and say enough is enough.
There can be no doubt that this is the worst crisis that the Canadian economy has faced since the 1930s. It is not just the continued closing of operations in Sudbury, Corner Brook or other parts of the Atlantic, the downturn in our agricultural economy, the crisis in our fishing industry which is the worst 1 have seen in my entire lifetime, or the state of the housing and forestry industries. It is also the heartbreak of hope deferred by millions of Canadians. The fact is that Government-announced turning points lead only to more disappointments.
Canadians are asking, in fear and in anger, just what is wrong with our country and our Government. Why are we in this deep depression in a land which is blessed with so many natural resources? There are, of course, many answers which could be given to that question, and some of them can be found in this Bill. This Bill calls for increased taxation of employee benefits, such as retiring allowances, employee loans, automobile benefits, deferred profit-sharing plans and personal service corporations, among other things.
To give Hon. Members some idea why 1 call this Bill a bureaucratic nightmare, I wish to place on the record, since many of my constituents will not have an opportunity to read the Bill, a sample of the wording found on some of this Bill's 295 pages as it applies to the standby charges to be paid by an employee to his employer for non-business vehicle use. I will begin on page 2 and quote only a few lines. On page 2 it is stated:
(2) For the purposes of paragraph (l)(e) an amount that is a reasonable standby charge for the automobile for the aggregate number of days in a taxation year during which it was made available by an employer or by a person related to the employer shall be deemed to be the amount equal to the product obtained when
(a) where the employer or the person related to the employer owned the automobile at any time in the year, an amount in respect of its cost to the employer equal to the percentage thereof obtained when 2% is multiplied by the quotient obtained when such of the aggregate number of days hereinbefore referred to as were days during which the employer or the person related to the employer owned the automobile is divided by 30 (except that if the quotient so obtained is not a full number and exceeds one it shall be taken to the nearest full number or, if there is no nearest full number, then to the full number next below it), or-
It goes on in this manner for two solid paragraphs. That must be the longest unfinished sentence in Canadian literature. It just boggles the mind. I ask the Minister and any Member of the Government, how can a Bill with this type of wording create stability, as stated by our Minister of Finance? That is the question I would like answered.
As if this were not confusing enough, the Bill goes on to other matters of taxation. But then, on page 25, it contains similar double-talk on the possible benefits of the company car, which are taxable if same is used by a shareholder. I ask, why were these measures not kept together, especially as they apply to automobile taxes? Of course, this is something that my mind, being that of an ordinary MP, will never understand, but it does explain one thing. It explains why every Canadian commercial traveller in Canada today is up in arms. He is literally unable to determine where he stands, what he must pay to his employer, and what he must do with the company car.
All of this type of taxation double-talk is deemed necessary in order to secure an ever-increasing amount of funds to pay the salaries of an ever-increasing number of civil servants. This horror story, and that is all I can think of to call it, was outlined in detail by Canada's Auditor General, Kenneth Dye, who pointed out in his Annual Report that not even Canada's federal Cabinet Ministers know for certain how a great deal of Canadian tax money is spent. To me, this simply does not make sense.
We have before us a Bill which seeks to plug every loophole, which seeks to get every possible penny from these working Canadians who are trying to keep this country going, while the same Government which deliberately plans to make our workers and their employers as wretched as possible takes no steps whatsoever to see to it that every tax dollar is properly and wisely spent. I ask the Government, through Your Honour, why is there this inconsistency? Why does the Government hit out so hard at the little taxpayer, but makes no
February 7, 1983

direct effort to try to curb the unnecessary expenditures of Crown corporations?
Here is what Mr. Dye, after two years of study, had to say: "My first impression of sprawling immensity, confusion of purpose and a sense of urgency comparable to the alacrity of a turtle, remains". On page 13 of his Report of March 31, 1982, Mr. Dye states that the problem of achieving accountability is massive in its dimensions. There are more than 300 Crown corporations, including subsidiaries, employing some 263,000 Canadians. Revenues of Crown corporations for the last fiscal year were $31.9 billion and expenses were $33.6 billion. That represents a loss in one year of $1.7 billion. These are taxpayers' dollars. Most of these corporations are virtually unknown, even to the best-informed Members of Parliament and Cabinet. Yet, in the aggregate, they represent a hole in the taxpayer's pocket, resulting, as they often do, in a consistent negative return on the taxpayer's investment.
Our Auditor General has stated that it might be helpful, in visualizing the state of the problem, to think of the whole group as an economic iceberg floating lazily on the foggy Atlantic, silent, majestic and awesome. As a Nova Scotian and as a Member of Parliament from Atlantic Canada, I can fully appreciate that analogy because 1 have seen those icebergs floating, awesome, silent and majestic, on the Atlantic; and I can assure Hon. Members that while they are awesome, they are also frightening. I think that is the comparison our Auditor General wished to make so that Canadians would better understand.
The public tends to see only the upper portions of icebergs, consisting of the giants like the CNR, Petro-Canada, CBC, Air Canada and Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. However, the great bulk of the iceberg below the surface is less spectacular, less likely to attract public interest, less likely to receive the attention of Parliament, yet costly to the taxpayer. Indeed, Mr. Dye says: "There seems to be, deep down near the bottom of the iceberg, subsidiaries of Crown corporations that may escape all public scrutiny".
This is the real reason behind the Bill. The Government does not seem to know how our tax dollars are spent, and its own concern is to find new ways of getting more taxes from those working Canadians who are still operating. 1 presume it is necessary, in order to keep these Crown corporations running, to have restrictive tax laws like those enshrined in Bill C-139, but I personally feel that we can no longer continue turning a blind eye and a deaf ear to Crown corporations which are losing close to $2 billion annually.
Mr. Dye did pinpoint some of the losses. He told us about a device which is called a "letter of comfort", under which a Minister is authorized by the Cabinet to support the credit of Crown corporations. The amounts involved can be significant. In the last six years, for example, more than $1 billion has been advanced to Canadair through a sequence of letters of comfort. The authorized limit is $1.35 billion. This amount of taxpayers' money is at risk without what I consider to be any real, clear criteria for providing continuing support or even for
Income Tax
discontinuing this kind of support. There is no assurance that $1.35 billion is sufficient.

speechtext: It is not.

speechtext:
In this period of severe recession, the Government support for such troubled companies as Massey-Fergu-son, de Havilland, Canadair, Maislin Industries and Dome Petroleum represents a very big risk. Why must the entire action be taxed to death, as in Bill C-139, for those favourite few? What are the names of the other companies, those which will belly-up to the trough to be spoon-fed by Canadian taxpayers' dollars, by this socialist Government?
The worst example of Crown corporation bungling, as outlined by our Auditor General, concerned the money made available by the Government to Petro-Canada for the purchase of Petrofina. This wholly-owned Crown corporation was used by the Government to identify, evaluate, recommend and negotiate the acquisition of Petrofina at a cost of $1.7 billion. It is one of the crimes of the Government that to date the Auditor General has not been able to assess whether the $1.7 billion invested by the Government of Canada for the purchase of Petrofina was expended with due regard to economy.
The Government feels that it must crack down hard on Canadians who may receive some amount of interest on life insurance policies purchased for the protection of their wives and families, in the event of their death, but it cannot give or refuses to give our Auditor General a detailed breakdown of the expenditure by Petro-Canada of $1.7 billion, which is an action which not only represents a callous disregard for our taxpayers' money, but one which is also affecting the very livelihood of the taxpayers from whom the money was originally taken. In my own constituency, 1 have small, independent service stations being put out of business by the unfair competition they face from stations set up by the Government Crown corporation.
When this Government is restricting tuition fees and educational deductions for young Canadians, it should ask itself why its basic accounting policies not only fail to produce a fair and honest representation of the Government's accounts, but, as reported in one case, it actually omitted $445 million of revenue that should have been included if the Government had followed its own rules. It should also inquire of itself why Government departments are still indulging in year-end spending sprees rather than turning back unspent funds at the end of the fiscal year. There is no reason why it could not do that. The Government should at least give an explanation to Parliament concerning the $219 million spent last year on overtime, even though most departments and agencies do not have adequate policies and guidelines governing the use of overtime. It should also explain why Canada is the only OECD country in the top ten in which industrial productivity has decreased.
This Government should want to know why it shows a deficit of $24 billion this year. With 24 million Canadians, that amounts to $1 billion for every one million people. If the

February 7, 1983
Income Tax
Americans had that type of deficit, they would be going crazy. There are 240 million Americans, but their predicted deficit is in the range of $180 billion. For their deficit to be comparable with Canada's deficit, it would have to be $240 billion. Perhaps this is one of the reasons our dollar is worth only 75 cents in the United States.
If the Government wants to know why inflation is still at a double-digit figure and unemployment rolls are still rising, I would say that it need look no further than this Bill. This Bill is a capsule form of the gross mismanagement of Canada by the present administration. It is the collective result of three budgets in one year, ail presented to Parliament without proper thought or planning by this administration. The result is a very uncertain direction for our ship of state. This state is in the same predicament as a ship whose captain is uncertain of his compass readings. When this happens in Atlantic Canada, the captain slows down his forward speed as he creeps along. He is constantly looking for some familiar headland or marker so he can get his bearings. This all takes time, and while the captain is in this state of uncertainty, there is little or no forward progress for his ship. This situation continues until an expert checks and brings the magnets in line so that it gives a true compass bearing.
In conclusion, 1 say that our captains of industry are no different from our sea captains. They will simply plod along slowly and warily until they are convinced that their compasses are reliable and giving them a true bearing. I submit that it is way past the time when this Government should give a true course to our captains of industry so we can go forward and progress together.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO STATUTE LAW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the object of taxation for any Government is to raise the necessary money required for the public purposes of the country, and the responsibility of a Minister of Finance is to organize the economy so that it produces the best result in terms of profitability and business activity that makes the collection of tax possible. The talent of a Minister of Finance should be used to run a goose farm where he makes sure that he can pluck feathers out of the geese without annoying them so that they stop laying the golden eggs. In any measure of ability in running a goose farm, this Government, this Minister, has "goosed" the country, has made sure that the production of golden eggs has been significantly reduced and has created nothing but hissing and upset by every faction of the country from business to labour and, indeed, as expressed earlier by the Member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen), even from the backbenchers of the Liberal Party.
The production we have before us, Bill C-139, is the result of a mess of budgets, November 12, June 26 and now this effort of October, all supposed to do something to make the economy of Canada work. In my view this Bill that we now have before us is a Bill that assists in preventing the economy
of the country from working, and therefore it should be significantly amended or withdrawn.
When the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) was first appointed to replace the former Minister, who was a disaster, he gave us some hope. He talked in glowing terms of the enterprise economy, how it should be the engine of growth, how we would get with it, how changes would be made that would make that enterprise economy work again. However, actions speak louder than words, and no sooner had the Minister finished his budget remarks in October than we proceeded to have $680 million of Petro-Canada money used to buy British Petroleum; we had further grants to Canadair and to de Havilland; we had the Maislin fiasco; we had the program for six and five that was supposed to reduce Government expenditures. At the same time the Minister came before us in the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs on his estimates, and he said that he had to increase the number of persons working in his department by 48, that he had to increase the total staff in his Department by 7 per cent and that he had to increase the total wages paid in his Department by 15 per cent.
That is really the Minister's attitude here. He says that we have to make the economy of Canada grow, and that this budget and these Bills are for that purpose. On the other hand, judging by what he does, we find that the $680 million to buy more service stations and the 15 per cent increase in the wages paid in his own Department is his appropriate response to restraint.
The tax system we have in the Income Tax Act is exceptionally complicated. It is not only complicated, it is confusing and complex. Indeed, the committee that studied the proposals of June were able to call many expert witnesses before it, and 1 want to read into the record a statement made by Donald Huggett, editor of the "Canadian Tax News", a Coopers & Lybrand publication. Donald Huggett is certainly one of Canada's most expert tax authorities, and he says:
I have specialized in tax work for almost 30 years, and the law is now incomprehensible to me in quite a few cases. It is, in my view, quite unconscionable to have a law that affects almost every adult Canadian and which is understood by only a handful.
I want to suggest that the Members of this House now debating this Bill, including myself, in large measure do not completely understand the Bill, not by a long shot. I want to say that almost every Canadian does not understand the Bill, including chartered accountants and lawyers who specialize in tax problems. We have a situation where we are trying to make the economy of our country grow and produce and increase in size, and we burden that economy with legislation that is incomprehensible to most people, that is contradictory in many cases, that has no general over-all thrust to it, and that is really difficult for anyone to understand on a philosophical basis, let alone any other basis.
What is it doing? I suggest this legislation is totally antiproductive. It is causing people to go into what is called the
February 7, 1983

black economy. People cannot understand the Bill, so why should they pay the tax in the first place? What they do is trade one good or service for another, my carpentry work for your dental work. This is going on to a greater and greater extent all the time. After this Bill passes, it will go on even more. That is the situation this Bill creates.
Let me give one example. We have the new 12.5 per cent tax on the distribution of corporate profits after the 1982 corporate year. What has happened? A great number of people who have small businesses have stripped out to private holding companies their pre-1982 surpluses so that they can pay those out without attracting the 12.5 per cent tax. More important, there is no longer any point in a small-businessman creating a surplus within his company to build the company. The effect of the 12.5 per cent distribution tax will put him in exactly the same position as though he earned the money in a personal way.
The Government says that is equitable, but the fact is that what we have been trying to do in taxation all along is to get small businesses to grow. What this statute does is prevent small businesses from growing. If small business takes advantage of the small business limit and lets the surplus grow, does anyone think that a small business will pay the 12.5 per cent distribution tax? Not unless they are really stuck or make a mistake.
What will happen is that the surplus will never be paid out, so the tax will never be paid. If the tax is never paid, there is no income tax paid by the proprietor which is attributable to his receipt of dividends. The Government will lose not only the tax on the dividends but will lose the build-up of the small business and never get the 12.5 per cent tax. That surplus will be leached out in some other fashion.
The Minister's officials know how this is done, as does the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres). However, they have not communicated that to the Minister of Finance and his officials. The truth is that his officials are all from the ivory tower. They do not understand how business works. They do not understand the motivation of people. They produced this absolutely ridiculous legislation that will hamper, hurt and hinder the development of this country and its small-business community, with no revenue gain for the country whatsoever.
The Minister says it is too difficult to simplify the Income Tax Act. He says we live in a difficult world and therefore we must have difficult statutes. He says that when we pass an Act and give a benefit, we create a loophole so we have to have anti-loophole sections, anti-anti-loophole sections and antianti-anti-loophole sections, until the Act is a foot thick, with rulings that run seven days from Sunday, almost all of which are incomprehensible.
We really do not need to have that condition. Is it necessary that Parliament be subjected to a statute that is so complicated that Members of Parliament, the accounting profession and the legal profession cannot read it? The Members of the Government who try to enforce the statute and the courts cannot read it. Is that really necessary? I say it is not.
Income Tax
Is there any reason why this Minister and this Government cannot appoint a task force committee of sensible people who are elected to this House, many with a good business background, representing constituents who are not from the ivory tower? They could go through this Act and change the system. Must we have a capital cost allowance system with 28 kinds of capital cost allowance?
Can we not integrate corporate and personal taxes so that we do not need to have various kinds of surpluses? Can we not have a situation where you either pay personal tax as your corporate tax or pay it as personal tax? It really does not matter. Can we not integrate personal and corporate income tax?
Do we really need to have tax on capital gains in view of the fact that the total receipt by the federal and provincial Governments from capital gains this year will probably be less than a billion dollars in all? Are the problems and complications in terms of reserves, all that we have heard about- annuities, evaluations, valuation dates and appraisers-all that necessary? Does any of that make Canada grow and build again? Do we really need some of the provisions in the Income Tax Act, bearing in mind that the purpose of taxation is to raise sufficient money for the legitimate purposes of the state in such a fashion that the goose does not hiss too much and continues to lay the golden eggs?
Speaking of the golden egg, we have seen what has happened to the economy of this country since the famous budget of November 12. The Minister may say that the problems of the economy are world wide, but it is strange that they are greater in Canada, and that Canada's performance in moving ahead is worse than that of 24 countries in the OECD. I suggest it is the ineptness expressed in Bill C-139 and in the budgets we have had that have been largely responsible for the lack of golden eggs being laid by our goose, the economy of Canada, a Canada to which we all belong, which we cherish and want to go forward.
In section after section, instead of wanting to make the country grow, this Government has shot itself in the foot. How can you expect people to invest if at the same time you take the capital cost allowance and cut it in half in the year when it is needed most? If a man buys a piece of machinery in order to improve the productivity of his plant, what does this Government do? It says that even though he has to pay for the machinery this year, he will not have as much tax allowance, tax holiday or tax deferral in the first year of purchase as was the case previously. In other words, the Government does not want him to buy more new equipment and be more productive. How does that work? How does it help the country grow? It does not.
The Government may pick up an extra billion dollars in revenue through corporate taxes, but when you look at the Government's own forecast for capital investment in real terms, it is down 8 per cent this year over last year and 6 per cent over the year before. As a result of that budget, capital acquisitions of a depreciable nature by companies in this

February 7, 1983
Income Tax
country are down at least 14 or 15 per cent. That kind of capital cost acquisition would have attracted the full capital cost allowance. Is there not some relationship between the capital cost allowance provided for in the old system and that now provided for, indicating that this reduction in the purchasing of capital equipment is taxed induced? I suggest there is.
Dealing with the MURB problem now, the Minister was worried that people were using deferred income arrangements to make themselves wealthy while building fancy apartment houses; therefore, these terrible things should be stopped. But rather than stop that type of action, which he could have, he decided to stop all soft costs. What is a "soft cost"? It is interest expended while you are getting a project going. If you want to make a very major capital expansion of a factory, you have to start spending money today on its plan and on the architects. Pretty soon you have to spend money to clear the land and to start building. It may be a two-year project in the course of building and in many cases all of that money has to be borrowed. Up until now, those who did that were entitled to deduct from their other income the interest spent in creating the project. Naturally, they were entitled to do that. That is the business way of doing things. But this budget says that under no circumstances can you deduct your soft costs from your other income unless you happen to be in the business of an apartment builder who can deduct it from his apartment income.
A man who wants to expand his factory has to borrow money for the course of construction and cannot deduct that interest from his business profits. He has to capitalize it. I say to you, sir, that in the case of a person who wants to expand his manufacturing potential, this tax provision, is costing him 20 per cent to 25 per cent more, and this is the kind of thing which is contained in Bill C-139.
The Bill is a disaster. It is anti-productive. The Government's attitude is anti-productive. It does not matter what the Minister says; what matters is what he is doing. If he really believed what he said in his economic statement speech, he would not have included this provision. But it is there because his bureaucrats do not understand how the business community works.
With respect to the matter of capital formation, for a long time there was a provision that if somebody sold a capital asset they could purchase an IAAC and defer the tax. They would have to invest the money. They would have to pay the tax eventually, but they would invest the money.
Second, there was a provision where people were encouraged to buy insurance. Somebody said, "Look, they are getting a tax advantage if they buy insurance; they are getting a tax advantage if they buy an annuity"-because you do not pay tax on the earned income derived from this type of investment as you go. You only pay the tax when income from the annuity or the deferred investment comes into your pocket. Therefore, you are supposed to receive a benefit. This kind of investment was building capital assets in Canada and was making money available for new investment. This Bill has shot the country in
the foot by depriving it of that new capital available for investment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe there are elements in that speech which are very disappointing. Similar comments were made by the Hon. Member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis) and the Hon. Member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse). We have heard three speakers this morning deliberately try to confuse the application of tax laws and the general state of the economy. For example, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) claims that a company will not buy new equipment because of changes in the capital cost allowance. That bald statement came from the Hon. Member as if somehow there is an economic environment in the country today which otherwise would warrant the purchase on a wide scale of new equipment. Yet we have heard from all kinds of groups that that is not true.
I would like the Hon. Member to focus in a little more on the distinction between the tax law, fair tax laws, and the general state of the economy. Could he now tell us why so many people in front of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs told us that the capital cost allowance will not stimulate or depress equipment sales because the state of the economy does not warrant such equipment sales at all? subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO STATUTE LAW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although there are nearly 300 pages of this Bill which contain a wide range of changes to the Income Tax Act, we should not be misled into thinking that the Bill represents any fundamental overhaul of our income tax system. Yet fundamental reform is what we need.
In opening the debate on December 13, the Minister said that the Bill represents a substantial structural change in the system. I dispute that, Mr. Speaker. Canada needs a tax system which supports and promotes the basic objectives of our society, and we need a tax system which is fair and, at least in its broad outline, can be understood by the general taxpayer. Now, I admit that what the Parliamentary Secretary said has

February 7, 1983
Income Tax
some validity, that there are certain sections which are naturally technical, but the broad outline should be able to be understood by the ordinary taxpayer.
Because our society is always changing, we must from time to time update our laws to take account of these changing conditions. But this has not happened for a long time and is not happening today. One of the reasons for that is detailed in Colin Campbell's book "The Canadian Senate: A Lobby from Within". He points out that as one of its most basic functions the Senate acts to protect the business community from any excess of democratic or egalitarian sentiment. Perhaps if Canadians ever get serious about tax reform their first act should be the abolition of the Senate, which almost invariably acts as the protector of property in opposition to the interests of the broad base of society.
Canada today needs a tax system that will work toward the following basic objectives. Number one, full employment. New Democrats believe that the total resources of society have to be mobilized in support of full employment. At a time when technological change combines with changing world markets to eliminate thousands of traditional jobs, we need to devote our best resources to solving the problems of unemployment. This will not happen, as the Tories say, by unleashing the private sector. That way lies chaos, and perhaps the best example of that is in the American truckers' strike where deregulation over the last few months has led to such cutthroat competition that thousands of small, independent truckers today are on the verge of bankruptcy.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, the Tories are so obsessed with the survival of the fittest ethic that they should consider who is fittest to survive in today's world. Perhaps even the Tories could conclude that the characteristic most needed for survival in today's world is co-operation, and that is just as true of individuals, communities and nations as it is of political parties. I fear that the Tories will be rather late in learning that.
Our tax system, Mr. Speaker, should facilitate community and national co-operation for such basic services as health care, pensions for senior citizens, Family Allowance, higher education, community and national security, the elimination of regional disparities and a sound economy. Furthermore, our taxes have to support our Government for regulation and policing of such areas as the environment and foreign investment. Our tax system should support and work toward these objectives. All Members of the House would agree with the need for fairness in our tax system, but we do not all agree on what is fair. New Democrats believe that the fairest system of taxation is a progressive income tax built on the basic concept that a buck is a buck, regardless whether it is wages or capital gain. Tax incentives should be seen as tax expenditures and subject to annual review by Parliament, the same as other expenditures, and they should be tied to performance.
In the past few years we have seen a trend whereby more and more of the tax burden has been shifted from corporations to individual taxpayers. In 1952, 53.7 per cent of tax revenue came from corporations. By 1972 this had shrunk to 26.6 per cent. For individuals, however, the process was reversed. In
1952 they paid 46.3 per cent of total tax revenue, but in 1972 that had increased to 73.3 per cent. There was a slight improvement in the balance by 1980 when 30.5 per cent of tax revenue came from corporations and 69.4 per cent came from individuals. The broad, basic imbalance continued, however.
The tax system should not only be fair, it should be understandable. In the explanatory notes to the Bill there is a section entitled "Death of a Taxpayer". That has a rather literary ring to it, reminiscent of Miller's "Death of a Salesman". When Willy Loman, the salesman, died, one of his sons said that he never knew who he was. If the taxpayer never quite knew who he was, usually there was a number that helped him get by- registration number, social insurance number, UIC claim number and so on. I am certain that the taxpayer never knew all the taxes he was paying, or did he know about all the possible exemptions, reductions and loopholes available to those with enough money to hire tax lawyers or accountants. He may have heard of the over 700 Canadians who had incomes of over $100,000 per year who never paid any income tax at all and wondered how they got away with it. His tax always seemed to be deducted at source. There is material in the title "Death of a Taxpayer" for some promising young Canadian writer to write a novel or a play. I gladly donate the idea.
The Bill before us does not begin to meet our basic objectives or our national needs of being fair and understandable. Rather than a fundamental overhaul of the tax system, this Bill is a thing of shreds and patches. On the coast we would call this "gunnysack" legislation because it seems as if everything is dumped together. One exemption is tied to another with a little bit of wire here and a loophole is patched with a bit of chewing gum there. The whole thing is gunnysack legislation.
In his opening remarks the Minister spoke of the need to end uncertainty, but in the last 18 months the Government has contributed a great deal to uncertainty in the tax system. In the last few weeks, nothing has contributed more to that uncertainty than the various kites flown by different Ministers. The latest and worst example occurred on January 2, when the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola), who is also responsible for the status of women, spoke on the TV program "Question Period" of eliminating the spousal exemption. On that program she made the following statement:
When we look at the whole system of family benefits, where are we going? One of the things that I think we are going to have to take a serious look at is the whole question of spousal deduction. What is happening in our soceity today is that women-as I say, 42 per cent of them are in the work force, and yet we are allowing a spousal deduction which I consider enourmous-it will be $3,300 this year-to slip out of our hands when, in fact, those families who are able to use the spousal deduction are up at the top end of the income scale. It's only the more affluent families in our society that allow a woman to stay at home, and I feel that we should examine that and perhaps somewhere down the line re-channel some of that into where I think the critical areas are, in child care.
I wonder where the Minister has been. She does not seem to understand the average family today. Her later retractions and attempts to clarify this have only increased the uncertainty that Canadians feel. Ordinary Canadian families do not think
February 7, 1983

that they need to be shafted by the Minister of State for Mines.
In his opening remarks the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) also said that he wants the Bill passed as soon as possible so that income tax returns can be processed and mailed out. Nobody knows better than we in the New Democratic Party the necessity of getting Government cheques out promptly to the ordinary people. There have been delays in processing superannuation cheques. Last week I had a letter from a constituent who complained that the last cheque received was dated December 19. The Government deliberately withheld those cheques as a form of blackmail, Mr. Speaker, and we do not want to see the same thing happen with income tax returns. On the other hand, this legislation is too important to be pushed through. The Government should forget its attempts at blackmail. Income tax returns should be mailed out. After all, the reduced Family Allowance cheques were mailed before the House had the opportunity to deal with the legislation.
In the few minutes remaining to me, Mr. Speaker, I want to concentrate on a couple of things that I think are most harmful to ordinary Canadians. The Minister said that the Bill is based on the principle that the Canadian tax system is better off with lower tax rates applied to a broader income base. I am sure all of us, and certainly all New Democrats, would agree with that as a general principle. But the way to broaden the base is surely to increase employment at decent wages. The Bill does nothing to broaden the base in that way; in fact, its effect is quite the opposite. The Bill broadens the base by capping the indexation of personal exemptions and then lowers the marginal tax rate for people at the upper end of the spectrum.
The entire six and five program has had the effect of driving down the real incomes of ordinary Canadians. We have had to oppose the cuts imposed by six and five on wages of public sector workers, Old Age Security, pensions for public servants and Family Allowances. Even without the capping of indexation for income tax exemptions, these measures will result in the removal of $1.16 billion from the pockets of ordinary Canadians and from the economy. The Minister admitted the need for some stimulation in the economy, but he continues to depress it with the six and five program.
The partial deindexing of personal exemptions will, in effect, be a tax increase of $1.7 billion in 1983-84. As with other aspects of six and five, this will penalize lower income people at a proportionately higher rate than higher income people.
A married taxpayer with two dependent children and an income of $20,000 per year will face a 21.7 per cent tax increase. The same taxpayer with an income of $100,000 per year will pay an increase of only 3.2 per cent. In a similar manner, the lower marginal tax rate will result in a real tax decrease for those in the upper income bracket.
Taxpayers with a taxable income of $133,440 and over per year will have their marginal tax rate brought down from 43 per cent to 34 per cent. Those with taxable incomes under $11,120 per year will receive no reduction at all in the marginal tax rate. They also suffer from the de-indexing program.
In short, Mr. Speaker, we oppose the Bill because it perpetuates and increases inequalities in the rate of taxation. It is not fair, and it does not address the fundamental problems of our society, which is the need for full employment. And certainly, Mr. Speaker, it will not result in a more understandable tax system.
