CROWSNEST PASS RATE-EFFECT OF CHANGES ON QUEBEC FARMERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there is not going to be a pork war because of the changes in the Crow rate. At the present time, western pork is not being brought to Quebec markets, although the selling price in the East is about $2 more than in the West. The reason is quite simple: The cost of shipping 100 pounds of pork meat from Calgary to Montreal is $8.51, which means a difference in price of $6.51 per 100 pounds. Under the new policy, western producers will be able to save on the cost of feeding their livestock which, according to the Department of Agriculture, will be $3.17 per 100 pounds in 1985-86. West to East will therefore continue to favour the competitive position of Quebec's pork producers.
It will, in fact, be practically impossible and certainly not worthwhile to ship pork from Calgary to Montreal, short of wanting to go bankrupt.
I would therefore suggest that Quebec farmers put the question to our political smart alecks, who are implying that the exact opposite will happen. This is the real challenge: to bring out the truth.

RATE OF UNEMPLOYMENT AMONG YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, concern for the unemployed has been voiced on a number of occasions. However, the heart of the matter, the young people, hardly ever receive enough consideration. 600,000	young Canadians out of work.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: THREAT OF RESIGNATION BY EDMONTON HEART SURGEON
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, a disturbing CBC report emanating out of Edmonton indicated that a surgeon specializing in cardiac surgery is planning to leave the country since he is frustrated by the failure of his hospital to provide him with adequate equipment and support facilities to carry out important operations in his specialty safely and effectively.
Cardiac surgery in children deals with reconstructive and reparative procedures correcting a variety of congenital malformations of the heart and large blood vessels. These operations are physiological for the most part, restoring normal anatomy and function of these organs and thus assuring a normal lifespan.
These operations require not only a well trained skilful surgeon but a team effort of medical and paramedical specialists as well as appropriate nursing staff. Not only in Edmonton but in many of the large communities, with teaching hospitals staffed with well trained and knowledgeable specialists, facilities are sadly lacking to carry out ever-increasing sophisticated procedures to improve the quality of life of our Canadian citizens.
In order that Canada may continue to remain in the forefront of world medicine, those charged with formulating the proposed Canada Health Act must provide optimum conditions for medical care, particularly for our doctors with specialty training, lest the system fall into mediocrity, and Canadians are deprived of the benefits of modern advances in the field of medicine and surgery.

Madam Speaker, I can tell the Hon. Member that there is a letter in the mail to him giving him a detailed answer to the question he raised. In summary, I would simply point out that one of the difficulties in the proposal he makes is that if someone simply goes on their own to apply for a training course, that in a sense contravenes the basic formula of the Unemployment Insurance Act, namely, that in order to collect benefits you must be available for work. We waive that requirement when someone comes into an employment centre and we have record of their willingness or preparedness to take a training course. We can waive that requirement because we have foreknowledge of their interest and intent.
If someone goes on their own account and registers for a program and then applies for UI, we have not had the opportunity to do an interview to determine their eligibility or any of the other criteria. speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Begin (Minister of National Health and Welfare) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TI ME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-132
speechtext:
That, in relation to Bill C-132, an Act to amend the Family Allowances Act, 1973, one sitting day shall be allotted to the consideration of each of the report stage and the third reading stage of the Bill; and
That 15 minutes before the expiry of the time provided for Government business on those days, any proceedings before the House shall be interrupted, if required, for the purpose of this Order and, in turn, every question then necessary in order to dispose of the stage of the Bill then under consideration shall be put forthwith and successively, without further debate or amendment.
Time Allocation
She said: Madam Speaker, I am introducing this motion for time allocation on Bill C-132, an Act to amend the Family Allowances Act of 1973, because I believe it is essential that this Bill receive the approval of this House as quickly as possible. Some may say that since we sent the Family Allowance cheque of January with an increase restricted to 6 per cent, it is no longer necessary to speed up debate and pass this Bill immediately. Well, we were given legal advice, of course, to the effect that we had the authority to send cheques to mothers with the 6 per cent indexation instead of full indexation. But that does not obviate the need for parliamentary approval.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TI ME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-132
speechtext: Why are you using closure, then?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TI ME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-132
speechtext:
I will explain in a few minutes, if Hon. Members want to listen and give me a chance to speak. We will not go on, say, until December, 1983. That would not be reasonable at all. I think the earliest possible passage of this Bill in this House and the other place is essential.
Hon. Members know that families, in this case mothers, were advised in the June budget of the six and five program, and specifically for that group of Canadians we would limit indexation to 6 per cent in order that everyone does their share to fight inflation and bring it down to the figures of six and five which we gave as our objective. When inflation was 12 per cent, we said to Canadians: "Let us try and bring it down to 6 per cent in 1983". It would have been 10 per cent the next year, and we said: "Let us try and bring it down to five in the year 1984".
Now, some people would say that the television, newspaper and radio commentary which always follows and explains a budget might not have been enough to make sure everyone was aware of the Government's plans. Therefore, in the August Family Allowance cheque I sent an insert which was short, quite clear and very factual, giving all the details to make sure that everyone understood the purpose of this decision of the Government. Since that time we have had, of course, several discussions in this House.
Now, I will come to the point of why it is so urgent to pass this Bill as soon as possible. Mothers were told that to make sure we were not creating any hardship, all mothers receiving the Child Tax Credit, either in full or part, would get an additional $50 on the coming Child Tax Credit to make up for any loss of indexation in the Family Allowance for the years 1983 and 1984.
Perhaps I should continue in French because I do not know quite how to say this in English.

The mothers are going to benefit from the provisions of Bill C-132, because in the last seven months, since last June, inflation has already dropped so far that the mothers who receive the Child Tax Credit, that is, those who need it, will be better off under this program.

February 7, 1983
Time Allocation

This additional $50 for all mothers receiving the Child Tax Credit-and let me point out this means two out of three mothers in Canada-is included in the Bill which follows mine, and that is why there is no reason my Bill should not be passed rapidly. It is contained in Bill C-139, an Act to amend the statute law relating to income tax. This is the main reason why any delay in passing Bill C-132 would prevent the mother receiving additional money through the Child Tax Credit in time. The forms have been sent but nothing can be paid out until Bill C-139 has been passed by the House.
There has been a lot of discussion on the Bill and I fail to see who could oppose it. When the Official Opposition was the Party in power, it wanted to abolish the universality of Family Allowances. That would be very dangerous, Mr. Speaker, but that Party has always wanted to do away with the program, never quite undertanding why it existed in the first place.
I think we are taking a rational approach in this Bill, and according to the mail 1 have received up to now, the vast majority of Canadians support it. We are saying that the country is in a difficult economic situation, as are all industrialized countries. The first objective is to fight inflation, to bring it down to 6 and 5 per cent to start with and then, as soon as possible, to lower it further. But we must not do this on the backs of those most in need, who in this case are the mothers.
Since there are many families that are single parent units, no one will get mad if all mothers with a Child Tax Credit, or a partial Child Tax Credit, receive an additional $50 to make up for the loss of full indexation of the Family Allowance. This is extremely generous, Mr. Speaker. We might have decided instead that the $50 additional provided in Bill C-139-which I hope will be passed very rapidly by the House to give that additional money to mothers-is very generous and should have been graduated to the mothers who get only a partial Child Tax Credit because the family income is over $26,000.
It is not often in today's society that children receive some benefit; it is usually given to the seniors. As the Minister is, in a way, the special voice of mothers in Cabinet in this case, looking out for the well-being of children, I am not going to oppose more money for the Child Tax Credit. Because it is a program which is targeted to those most in need, it means a benefit for very low-income mothers. It also means that those on the threshold of the middle class, the people who will be in the real middle class later, the young couples with young children who do not yet have enough money to meet all the expenses incurred in bringing up a family, will benefit.
I am sure that all Members of the House will recognize the fact that 32 Members have been involved in discussions over the last few weeks, back to last fall, when we started discussing the Bill in the House, and in committee where we heard witnesses. I should like to thank the Chairman and members of the committee, as well as the witnesses that were heard, for their contributions. It is surprising that the debate has already
occupied so much time of the agenda of Hon. Members. I hope the Bill receives speedy passage in order that we may proceed to Bill C-139 and ensure a better Child Tax Credit to two-thirds of Canadian mothers.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TI ME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-132
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say that the arguments of the Minister on why the Government has to apply allocation of time, or closure, to this Bill do not add up to much. First of all, we know that regardless of what Parliament does, the minute the officials who run this country see an excuse for a tax change to be introduced through a Ways and Means motion or any other method, they immediately apply it whether it is passed or not. That has been the practice for 30 years so I am not going to get into that argument now.
I am glad the Minister is in the House because she knows and understands what I am about to say. Bill C-132 regarding Family Allowances is another attack on the families of Canada. Families cannot be divided according to their wealth. Over and over again Parliament has tried to find a way to apply a means law. When the last major amendments to this Act were brought in, all parties agreed that the plan should be universal and the only means test should be the application of the Income Tax Act on a progressive scale.
I return to my First statement, Mr. Speaker. This attack on the family is small in terms of dollars and cents. The Minister made a good case that for those earning less than $26,000 per year the Government would try to compensate them for the loss in the Child Tax Credit. She is quite right in that. But the principle of this legislation is that it is part and parcel of a policy of rationalization by the senior mandarins of the civil service who cannot appreciate that when you apply a rational thought, it must be applied with equity and justice. I do not care whether a family has an income of $10,000 or $30,000 per year, Mr. Speaker. Under the laws of Parliament, regardless of the wealth of the parties they receive the Family Allowance. That is what Parliament ruled, supported by every Party.
The history of this is long, Mr. Speaker. During the days of the last war, politicians in all western countries sought to build the morale of their troops engaged in war who worried about their families at home. In the United Kingdom there was the Beveridge Report and in Canada the Marsh Report. All the mandarins of the civil service of the day, who were growing in power, accepted the proposition. In 1942 the concept was introduced and the starting place was the family. There was debate and, of course, division of opinion. Finally, every Member of the House voted for it, with one exception.
I was one of the then young men who was asked for an opinion. I was going overseas, leaving two young children and a wife at home. If I did not come back my wife and family would get a pension of $50 per month. I knew I would be much happier if there was something for the children when they were growing up. All parties accepted the document.
With this latest move, in the interest of restraint we would reduce voluntarily, and in some cases compulsorily, the
February 7, 1983

increased income of some people in order to help control inflation. The Party I speak for agreed to the six and five proposal for those who were making money and contracts were altered to that effect.
Common sense, equity and justice, however, say that this should not be applied to people who cannot defend themselves. The amounts involved are small but the principles involved are great. Every Member of Parliament has had a shame riding on his back for the last eight or ten years that he cannot get rid of. The Minister knows what it is and I know what it is. We pass laws based on our best reasoning, and when those laws are ignored by our masters, the mandarins who run the country, we say nothing and do nothing. The only person on the other side of the House that I have ever seen admit the discrimination and injustice of it is the Minister. This matter does not affect the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) or the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) because they know who their masters are and who they have to obey. These great rationalists who think they know how better to run the country say that six and five should be applied to everyone regardless of justice, equity or morality. They will do it.
1 want to return to the key thought. Under the morality of this Parliament, we decided that regardless of wealth every child up to 16 years of age, and 18 years of age if attending school, would receive Family Allowances. This decision by Parliament is being ignored every day by the irrational mandarins who run the country and who run Cabinet. Sure, the Bill will go through. Sure, they will put closure on it. But as they apply closure, let their conscience recognize that they will carry this scar until they die.
I am not unaware of the fact that we tend to be fraudulent and full of scam as Members of political Parties, but on occasions such as this let us face the fact that we are rushing through this Bill for the convenience of a few people who want it out of the way. It does not make any difference to the cheques going out or the amounts of the cheques. We in Parliament have a duty. This is a talking place and we have a right to talk in this place until every soul in Canada has heard our voice. But that voice will never be heard as long as others who want to be masters decide that no news of this parliamentary debate gets out to the people of Canada. Until every family in Canada has a chance to hear why those of us on the Opposition side are opposed to this legislation, we have a right to continue talking. Until the media realizes that it must tell the story of what is happening in the House, we will continue battling and fighting.
I am as ashamed as I know the Minister is that we continue discrimination against teenagers. Now we are loading an extra burden on families. Families are under attack all over the world, but no place are they more under attack than on the North American continent. The families for who we should be fighting, regardless of race, nationality, colour or religion, are the one institution around which we must all rally to protect at
Time Allocation
every turn. We are not protecting them in letting this perhaps small but significant amount go through.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TI ME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-132
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TI ME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-132
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise and address the House on this critical issue this afternoon. 1 watched very carefully as the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) stood up and called upon Members of the House to support this motion applying time allocation or closure. I watched her very closely. I listened very carefully to the words she used. I noticed a quaver in her voice as she delivered her words. I listened carefully to the way she phrased her sentences and I noticed that there was a lack of commitment in what she was saying. Also I noticed there was uncertainty in some of the points she was making. I watched her body language and noticed that she was not looking directly at Hon. Members opposite when she was speaking. I noticed that she was using body language, in a sense, to communicate the following to Members of the House: "I do not believe in what I am saying, I do not believe in the words that I am uttering. What I am saying is to be disallowed or ignored because it is not what I want to say, but I am forced to stand up and say it because the Government, senior mandarins or certain Cabinet Members have forced me to rise in the House of Commons to muzzle Parliamentarians from speaking out against a Bill which will deindex Family Allowances".
It is not surprising that the Minister spoke in a quavering voice. She understands clearly what the Bill is communicating to Canadian citizens from the East Coast to the West Coast. I have listened carefully to Ian Sinclair, chairman of the blue chip committee which is to advise the Government on the six and five program. Mr. Sinclair said that the six and five program was really causing damage to the economy of Canada, that we must take steps to encourage economic development to stimulate the economy, and that strangling more life out of the economy was not in our short-term or long-term best interests.
Then I looked carefully at a man who presumably advised the Government often on these matters, the Governor of the Bank of Canada. I noticed what he did to his retirees. He indicated that he did not believe in the six and five program, and for that reason the increase in their pensions this year will be 11.5 per cent, not 6 per cent or 5 per cent. Anyone would know that now is not the time to identify a group of women and children in Canadian society and ask them to bear the attack against inflation.
The Minister indicated that she put the mothers of the children of Canada on notice back in the June budget, that they knew it was coming and therefore it should presumably legitimize today's action of closing off debate on this particular Bill in Parliament.
I recall other Members, particularly on the Government side, saying that they have not received a landslide of letters from mothers or from thousands of children writing in about the decreases in the Family Allowances which they would have expected starting in January. Of course they have not, for two

February 7, 1983
Time Allocation
reasons. First, the mothers of Canada are not organized and do not become involved in letter-writing campaigns, as do certain other well-organized lobby groups. Certainly the children of Canada do not. But more important, 1 do not believe that the mothers of Canada believe or believed that the Government would do this. After all, they know they were not one of the causes of inflation. The paltry Family Allowance cheques which went out every month were not fuelling inflation. I suspect they heard in the budget discussions that indeed the Government would delimit the indexing of Family Allowance payments and they simply refused to believe it, it seemed so incredible. Then the Minister of National Health and Welfare said: "Listen, while we are reducing your income on this side, we will increase it on that side through subsequent legislation on the Child Tax Credit". She said that they would pass legislation some time in the future that would provide an increase in the Child Tax Credit to compensate for this loss.
This is asking a great deal of the Canadian public. They listened to the previous Minister of Finance who on occasion after occasion stood up and made promises. First he said that he would tax dental programs for employees. Later he changed his mind and said that he would not do it, that he would tax medical premiums. Then he again changed his mind and said that he would tax investment money used by people to purchase Canadian stocks. Then he changed his mind again. The previous Minister of Finance changed his mind 37 times. Yet the Minister of National Health and Welfare advises confidence in the Government because it will deliver what it says. I believe that is asking too much of the people of Canada, to have faith in a Government that has let them down on so many occasions.
We should consider what is happening today from another perspective as well. It deals with the psychology of the Canadian society. Today we have a country that is looking for strong political leadership. Canadians realize that our economy is floundering. We are like a ship at sea with no rudder. One day we lurch this way, and the next day we lurch back that way. We see a Government of Canada that is going from crisis to crisis. It tries one program, then another, tries a stimulus here while raising taxes there, gives a tax break to upper income earners and increases taxes to the middle income Canadian. We see a Government that is obviously out of control.
The people of Canada are asking for strong political leadership at this time. They are saying that we need someone who will stand up to show us where the problems are in our economy and how to fight inflation, and how to stimulate the economy. They want someone who will tell us how to encourage investor and consumer confidence. What the people of Canada do not want is a Minister who stands up in the House of Commons to say that the Government wants to take money from the mothers and children of Canada during these difficult times. The Government does not want to hear any more debate in the House of Commons on this issue and therefore introduces a measure called time allocation to cut off the
debate on this issue and to muzzle particularly Members on the Opposition side of the House to prevent them from pointing out the shortcomings of this legislation and pointing out the shortcomings of the political leadership that this legislation demonstrates.
There are dozens of countries in the world that envy a Parliament such as ours where people can hear two or three points of view on an issue. They can then draw their own conclusions on the subject in the comfort of their own home or workplace. It is important that the people of Canada have an opportunity to hear the various sides of an issue. We have heard some very convincing arguments as to why this legislation that will remove money from mothers and children of Canada is not the appropriate step to be taken at this time.
I remind Members of an earlier time when I indicated that the Chairman of the blue chip committee said that it is now time to change from this paranoiac adherence to the six and five program. The best thing this Government could do is to send a clear signal to Canadians across the country that in the interests of fair play and justice it will pull out this particular Bill that is before us now and, more important, will not go ahead with de-indexing of Family Allowance payments.

We have heard the Members of the Opposition speaking of everything except Bill C-132. This is certainly not a good use of Parliament's time. I ask, what is the purpose of parliamentary reform as expressed in the amended standing orders of December 22, 1982?

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TI ME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-132
speechtext: I would like to know.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TI ME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-132
speechtext: This is certainly not good use of parliamentary time.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TI ME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-132
speechtext: You brought in closure three times in three weeks.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TI ME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-132
speechtext: The purpose of parliamentary reform is to make Parliament more effective and better able to respond directly to the needs and wants of Canadians.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TI ME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-132

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TI ME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-132
speechtext:
However, if we insist on wasting our time by constantly repeating arguments that are many times filled with misinformation and allegations that are wrong, then we are not using Parliament effectively. We are not representing the concerns of our constituents who elected us. We are in fact hampering the whole parliamentary system and its effectiveness.
We have had similar debates regarding the whole question of time allocation in the past. The Hon. Member for Guelph
February 7, 1983

(Mr. Schroder) stated in the House on December 2, 1982, that:
Time allocation is a good management tool ... it apportions the time effectively.
I agree with the Hon. Member completely. Given the speeches from the Opposition during this debate, they are not putting their time to good use. In fact, they are attempting to score political points by misinforming and misrepresenting what in fact the Bill is all about. I hear Opposition Members screaming that we are imposing closure. The Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) used that work today. The Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) used that word today, saying it was closure.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TI ME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-132
speechtext: Three times in three weeks.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TI ME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-132
speechtext: There is a difference, and a very important one at that, between closure and what we are proposing now, that is time allocation.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TI ME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-132
speechtext: What is the difference?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to take part in this debate this afternoon for two reasons. One, I would like to say something about the whole idea of time management or management procedures, or whatever you want to call it, and I would like to talk a little bit about the fact that the psychology of inflation is important. I would like to talk about what effect the six and five program is having on the development of the momentum that is helping to reduce inflation.

February 7, 1983
Time Allocation
It is interesting that in this management of time the question is, have we had enough time to discuss this Bill? In second reading, we have had two hours and 45 minutes of debate. We have had 16 speakers, seven have been from the Official Opposition, five from the New Democratic Party and four have been from the Liberals. Now, at report stage, we have had six hours of debate. We have had 19 speakers, six Progressive Conservatives, 11 NDPs and two Liberals. That means that so far we have had 35 speakers. Of this the breakdown is: 13 Progressive Conservatives, 16 New Democratic Party Members and six Liberals, and the total time so far has been 12 hours and 30 minutes.
That, I think, indicates that there has been ample time for discussion of this Bill, but the other point that I think is important is the fact that the essence of this Bill really does not require the approval of Parliament, but the Child Tax Credit addition of $50 across the board, a once in a lifetime allocation of $50, does require the passage of Bill C-139, which is the Bill to amend the Income Tax Act. In order for this $50 to be available for the Child Tax Credit this year, which will help those who are most in need to cope with the situation of having to help us in this fight against inflation, it is very important that this Bill be passed.
We have heard a lot of discussion about inflation, and I do not profess to be an expert on the economics of inflation. If what I read is true, there are many different opinions about why we have inflation, and a great number of opinions about what is the best way to attack inflation. In essence, what we have been saying is that there are two ways in which we have to combat inflation. One of those is that the world recession has to be brought under control. Most of us know the very complicated reasons that are given for the fact that all countries in the western world, each of them having a different kind of government from ours, are all suffering from degrees of inflation, so we have this recession which is affecting the world in total. What we do in Canada is not going to have much effect on world matters concerned with inflation. That is not to say that we should not be doing something in Canada about inflation, helping to correct inflation in this country and helping people to cope with inflation.
What we did was to introduce the so-called six and five program in an attempt to cope with inflation in Canada and reduce the rate at which inflation was increasing, reducing it eventually from 12 per cent to 6 per cent this year and 5 per cent the following year. That is what the six and five program is all about. In other words, it is a first step in Canada toward economic recovery. It is not the only action necessary to turn the economy around, but it is the primary initiative in working toward this goal.
With regard to the six and five program and employment, a reduction in inflation is the key to economic recovery. That
includes securing those jobs we already have and creating new jobs. The Government job-creation program should be seen as a spin-off of the six and five program.
The emphasis of the six and five program has been on the urgency of getting inflation down. As inflation is reduced, consumer confidence and spending is encouraged and unemployment levels will gradually reduce or decrease. There are other purposes that are part of the six and five program, such as trying to bring down retail prices. We are having some success. The Consumer Price Index dropped to under 10 per cent in December 1982, the first time since March 1981. It dropped to 9.3 per cent.
Interest rates have decreased steadily. Interest rates of course have a tremendous impact on the construction and housing industry. We have seen what has happened with regard to restraint on federally-administered prices. We have established this in federal Departments, agencies, Crown corporations and regulatory bodies.
Wage settlements have decreased since the beginning of the six and five program. In fact, they have decreased substantially. This will decrease prices and will certainly foster Canada's competitiveness internationally.
What does this have to do with the Bill we are talking about today and the five Bills we are trying to get through this House which are related to the six and five program? The Opposition Members say we cannot continue to blame other countries for what is happening in Canada. They say we cannot continually refer to the world recession. That requires a degree of leadership. We must answer the question whether there is any light at the end of that tunnel or, as is often expressed, is there any hope?
This is why we are asking Canadians to enter this fight against inflation. This is why we have Bill C-132 to limit the indexation of Family Allowances to 6 per cent this year and 5 per cent next year. This is why we are asking Canadian families to accept this as their contribution in the fight against inflation.
We know that inflation unsettles the confidence of all, but no people more than the families of Canada. I was particularly interested in hearing Opposition Members suggest that somehow or other the mothers of Canada would not be able to understand the need for the six and five program. I say, who better than the mothers who are the managers of the families in this country, who better would realize that reducing inflation will make it easier for them to manage?
The purpose of this debate is to discuss the Bill rationally. It is to give the people of Canada an indication that this is a small price for them to pay for bringing about economic recovery and growth which, as the Minister says, will directly benefit all families by protecting them from the ravages of inflation and the resultant erosion of their budgets.

Mr. Speaker, this is the third time since January 17 that this Government has decided to use the hammer for limiting time for debate. The concept of the new rules we are supposed to be operating under is to limit the time for debate by shortening speeches on report stage to ten minutes. Consequently, this motion by the Government with respect to time allocation, certainly at report stage, is inappropriate. Indeed, by the very time limitations, Members' speaking opportunities would have run out very soon had the Bill been allowed to follow the normal course.
Second, there has been no indication by this Government of the extent to which consultations were held with respect to reducing the number of speeches or setting some time when this Bill would come to a vote.
It is a sad day for this House when we have the situation where, in the middle of an income tax debate or a day set aside for an income tax debate, a Minister of the Crown rises to impose time allocation in order to limit the length of debate. It is the third time this has happened since January 17. It is disgraceful management of the House by this Government. The new rules are supposed to make the House operate better
Time Allocation
and make it more relevant. However, the Government uses every opportunity to ensure that these new rules do not work.
This is one of a few Bills where the Government has gone ahead and operated as though it had legal authority to do so. It has already proceeded to reduce Family Allowances. Cheques sent out in January and presumably those prepared for February are at the reduced amount. The Government says it has legal authority to do that. The Government says it does not have to straighten up the question of indexing under the present Act until December, according to the Government's own legal opinion, to handle this matter and the question of the change in the amount of the Family Allowance.
The Minister has come to this House and said in public that there are three kinds of tax measures which affect people with families. Indeed, there are probably four, and I want to point those out to this House. First, there is the allowance for children under the Income Tax Act which goes to everyone who files an income tax form on a positive basis. That is an indexed amount. It has been changed, but there is an allowance which everyone who pays positive income tax receives toward the maintenance of their children, an income tax deduction. Second, the Child Tax Credit is another form of tax allowance for children which happens to be a positive credit. Even if you do not pay income tax, you receive this positive credit of up to $342, approximately, per child. The third allowance has something to do with the spousal allowance when there is, perhaps, a single parent who declares one of the children as, indeed, a spouse. A further allowance is available there. In addition to that, Mr. Speaker, there is an allowance for babysitting or child care help to families in the tax Act.
All of these matters should be brought together into one form of allowance for children. Both the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) and the Minister responsible for the status of women have spoken in the last weeks on these vital tax matters. There is ample time for this whole matter to be resolved by Parliament before December of this year, yet this Minister crashes ahead with a program which she knows does not make sense. There is no justification whatsoever on this particular Bill for any time allocation, particularly in view of the statements made publicly by the Minister responsible for the status of women and the Minister of National Health and Welfare with respect to comments concerning the Income Tax Act. The matter should be reviewed, and reviewed completely.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister spoke about the six and five program. We all know that that is a great, big advertising gimmick which has absolutely nothing to do with the cost of the national revenue, with the cost of Government, in this particular case. This Bill is being forced through because it is part of a general pattern, and the Government does not want to change or alter its pattern. There is no justification for forcing this particular Bill through, repeating six and five, six and five, six and five. Be damned to six and

February 7, 1983
Time Allocation
five. This Bill has not a heck of a lot to do with six and five at all.
The truth of the matter is there is a large increase in the amount of money being allocated to children by the Child Tax Credit in the Income Tax Act. There is an attempt to take some of it back in this amendment. The problem is that the Child Tax Credit is part of the Income Tax Act. The benefits under the Child Tax Credit go to mothers who file, or happen to file, income tax returns. In order to get the child income tax credit, you have to file the return. But when do you get the money? When the Government decides to pay out the credit a cheque is delivered which is part of an income tax rebate system, and it is a lump sum cheque.
The advantage of Family Allowance is that the cheque comes monthly to the mother. The money then can be spent monthly for the benefit of the children. The Child Tax Credit is a lump sum payment which can be used to put a downpayment on an automobile, go on a holiday, and perhaps have absolutely nothing to do with the support of children. The advantage of the Family Allowance system is that it is a monthly system, and if we are going to rely on the Child Tax Credit then it should be paid monthly to those persons who need the money to buy groceries. They do not just buy groceries in May and June when tax rebates are paid. They buy groceries in September, October, December and January. That is when they need the money. To say that the increase in the Child Tax Credit somehow is going to help families look after their kiddies is just wrong. It is not going to help them. It is a bureaucratic method of trying to solve these problems by tax adjustments, which cannot be done. What you have to do is to make sure the money is put into the hands of parents on a monthly basis so they can properly look after their current monthly bills for food, shelter, and so on. This is important to the maintenance of children. I say to the Government, therefore, this Bill is ill conceived, has not been thought out properly, does not properly address the question of maintenance of children, and does not properly reflect the payments which should be made to families to help them maintain their children.
There is ample opportunity before December of this year for the Government to form a committee to study the matter and to produce proper legislation which addresses the question of how we pay and how we look after those who are raising families, to make it more equitable for them in our society. This Bill does not do that. The proposal in Bill C-139 does not do that. It is a hodge-podge. It is a flim-flam.
The Parliamentary Secretary says it has something to do with inflation. Goodness, how are you going to solve inflation, by taking off maybe a couple of dollars from someone who gets a Family Allowance cheque, which is taxable in any event, and at the same time increasing the Child Tax Credit, so the net result of payment out by the state and payment into the state through the tax system is almost the same anyway?
Actually, Mr. Speaker, the Bill does not address the question of inflation. It does not address the question of fairness. It
does not address the question of the requirement to support children. It does not really deal with the issues at all. It is the kind of Bill which should be subject to a long debate for the very reason we have Parliaments. When you have bad legislation it should be exposed to debate by the people of Canada. The Parliamentary Secretary says we have spent 12 hours and 30 minutes. If that amount of time entitles the Government to foreclose an important issue like this, then there is something wrong with Parliament and with this Government in the way it is directing the affairs of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased with this opportunity to express my support, not only for Bill C-132 but also for the Hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mrs. Begin), and for her motion for time allocation, so that we can exercise our democratic right to vote either for or against certain measures.
I agree with the Hon. Member who spoke just now that Bill C-132 alone is not the answer to getting rid of inflation. This Bill is only one in a series of measures we must take at a time of serious economic difficulty, if we truly want to bring down inflation and put the economy back on its feet. I know that our friends opposite are not interested in supporting measures that will help to reduce inflation, because to them it is not good politics. It is not good politics to be positive. Consistently, they have always preferred to be negative-in other words, they criticize without offering alternative solutions.
Since Bill C-132 was first tabled in the House, thirty-five Members have taken part in the debate on this Bill, including sixteen from the socialist group. And yet there are Members who insist that the Minister of National Health and Welfare has no justification for using Standing Order 82. We on the Government side want to discharge our responsibilities, even if it is not always the popular thing to do. It is not popular to say that we are going to cap increases in family allowances, but we must not forget that the families who stand to suffer most, namely, those on low incomes and especially families with several children, will receive an increase of $50 per month in their child tax credit. That is far more than the amount they will have to give up as a result of capping at 6 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words about Standing Order 82 which we are invoking today. Considering the almost systematic obstruction practised by our two opposition parties, I submit that it might be necessary to invoke Standing Order 82 whenever we table a Bill. Between now and the end of this session, there are still a number of Bills to be passed, including several money Bills, and I think it is irresponsible of the Opposition to hold up the proceedings. I am accusing them of irresponsibility, as I did on the evening of July 8, when I tendered my resignation as Deputy Chairman of Committees of the Whole House. The Members opposite are not acting as true representatives of this country, that is what I said that evening, and I say it again today. You may recall the incident
February 7, 1983

on July 8 when the Progressive Conservative Members themselves had requested a vote and then left the House and did not come back.
Not so long ago, the NDP Members asked for a vote. They also left the House and did not come back.
The Canadian electorate did not give them a mandate to form a government. They were given a far more limited mandate, in keeping with their talents, namely, to provide opposition, not obstruction, which has become a habit among the Members of the NDP and their Progressive Conservative friends. We on the Government side want to discharge the responsibilities we have been given by the Canadian people. To do so, we are obliged to limit the time spent on debate, and I submit, with due respect, that this should become common practice as long as Members who are given a mandate to provide opposition insist on using that mandate to obstruct the proceedings of this House. On this side, if we are to be worthy of the trust of our electorate, we shall have to invoke Standing Order 82, whenever a Bill is tabled. Let us not forget that these irresponsible people held up the proceedings of the House for two weeks during the bells incident. I, for one, have not forgotten, Mr. Speaker. I had your job, and according to the Rules, the Chair had to be occupied twenty-four hours a day, and so it was. We did our duty. During those two weeks, the Liberals remained faithful to their mandate, and every day they came to the House, as required by the Rules. What did the Progressive Conservatives do during that time? They were travelling across Canada. You would have thought it was an election campaign. Mr. Speaker, although there is no legal obligation on these Members to return the salary they unlawfully received, 1 maintain that if they had any moral sense at all, they would pay back the compensation they received during the two-week walkout or should I say cop-out, because the latter expression is probably more appropriate.
The Opposition Members scream wolf every time that time allocation is invoked. They seem to forget that every Standing Order has a reason for being, in this case to protect us from the systematic obstruction we have seen in this House over the last two years. We have demonstrated on numerous occasions that if the Opposition has any concrete and positive propositions, we will gladly accept them. However, they seem to favour the negative approach, to the detriment of the people who have elected them.
Let us dispose of Bill C-132 and move on to other legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today with a sense of deja vu. It seems that every second time I rise to speak in this House, the subject matter is again closure. This is the sixteenth time that closure or time allocation has been imposed on the House of Commons during a single
Time Allocation
session. I can assure you that it has not been mindless opposition, such as we have just been accused of by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Ethier). The Opposition in this House has been doing an excellent job of showing up the weaknesses in the Bills presented by the Government. It is because of this responsible opposition and because the Government is unable to refute the facts and arguments we have advanced, that it finds it necessary to use closure on so many occasions.
Bill C-132, Mr. Speaker, which deals with Family Allowance, is part of the great six and five propaganda scheme. It is part of this great public relations gimmick the Government hopes will allow it to take credit for any reduction in the rate of inflation. Of course, that is happening not because of anything the Government has done, but because we are faced with a recession, a recession which was caused by the Government opposite. That is why inflation is abating somewhat. But the very policies pursued by the hon. gentlemen and hon. ladies opposite will guarantee that once the recession is over, we will again face a period of rapid and worsening inflation. Under this so-called six and five system we have a chicken and egg situation. We are faced with inflation and we know everyone has to cut back a little, but who goes first? It is pretty evident that, in the opinion of the Government opposite, it is the little guys who have to go first. It is not the Liberal fat cats who are going first, it is the little guy, the Family Allowance recipients, the pensioners, whether old age pensioners in general or Public Service pensioners in particular. It is the little guys who have been used by the Liberal Government as cannon fodder in the war against inflation.
We on this side of the House do not approve of those tactics, Mr. Speaker. We spent about 12 and a half hours on this debate before the Government decided to impose closure. That time should not have been used to discuss this rather nitpicking Bill, as the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blen-karn) has explained. After all, it is very much a matter of taking a little bit here from the Family Allowances and adjusting the Child Tax Credit, all with no real net effect on Government revenues or expenditures. What we should have been using that time for was a debate on the entire Family Allowance system.
This debate was opened not that long ago by the Minister responsible for the status of women who made certain proposals, which certainly did not go down too well in my part of the country nor, I think, in others. But at least the debate was open. The question arises: should we have the universal system of Family Allowances we now have in Canada? There are arguments pro and con. Personally, I do not really need the Family Allowance, but maybe there are a number of people in Canada who do. Perhaps a better system would be to give the money at present paid to people like myself to people who really need it. We might care to look at changes of that order.
We have problems with the taxability of Family Allowances. Each month the Government mails out literally millions of cheques right across Canada, and then on April 30 of the

February 7, 1983
Time Allocation
following year you get stuck with paying a lot of that money back again. The system of monthly cheques may not be the best one for many people who may prefer the yearly reconciliation at the time of filing their income tax return. Perhaps there should be an option so that people could choose the system they want. That would save millions of dollars as Canada Post would not have to send cheques all over the country.
I have brought this matter up in committee several times but it seems that the Government is reluctant to even consider the idea of changing the system of issuing monthly cheques. The reason for this is quite apparent, Mr. Speaker. It wants that federal cheque to go into practically every household in the country, to show what a good job it is doing. It is another part of the public relations and porkbarrelling that is so often engaged in by the Government. I would have a much greater appreciation of a federal Government that did not insist on sending a piece of paper to every house every month. When it comes to improving relationships between the Government and citizens, I think the provincial or municipal level is a better place to foster this. The federal Government should look after those things that properly fall into the federal domain.
These are some of the arguments that can and should be used in a full debate on Family Allowances rather than the debate we are having today, Mr. Speaker. There are much better ways to look after the interests of children than the system which presently exists.
In the few minutes remaining to me, Mr. Speaker, I should like to return to the matter of closure. Of the 16 times that closure or time allocation-which is the euphemism for it- has been applied, at least half have been unnecessary. Usually the debate was about to end anyway but the Government brought in closure to show who was boss. It wanted to show that it could call the shots. That is the sole reason closure was applied on those occasions. I suggest that that is a dangerous precedent because familiarity breeds contempt. The House and the country is becoming so familiar with closure that they no longer take any notice of it.
I suggest that the House leaders of all Parties get together and work out a system of agreement on the time allocated for debate on Bills of the nature of the one today. Closure is a copout, and I guess this Party has been guilty from time to time as well, but not too often. I will pursue this point the next time there is a debate on closure, Mr. Speaker.
In closing my brief presentation, I want to say that I am not satisfied that closure is warranted on this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to take the first two minutes of my address to rebut the remarks of the previous speaker regarding time allocation and closure. He did not think that closure was necessary on Bill C-132. Part of the problem that we have had on this side of the House during debate on second reading, committee stage and report stage, is the seeming inability of the Opposition to offer a comprehensive reply to the substance of Bill C-132. In the first six minutes of his speech the Hon. Member confused time allocation and closure, but there is a substantial difference
between the two, Mr. Speaker. It seems to me that this inability to distinguish is indicative of many of the contradictions in the speeches of Members of the Opposition regarding Bill C-131 and Bill C-132.
This afternoon the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) referred to the number of Members who have spoken since the Bill was introduced. At last count some 35 Members had participated in debate, including 16 Members of the Official Opposition. In order to effect speedy passage of the legislation, only nine Liberals have spoken.
It seems to me that a lot of misinformation has been given out by Members of the Opposition both in this Chamber and at committee. Nowhere in the debate has the Minister or any Member of this Party said that the reason for six and five being introduced on the Family Allowance, was to save money. Since the budget of June 1982, we in this Party have said that we are primarily concerned with an attack on the inflationary psychology that seems to have gripped the Canadian public. We realized that if we were to live in an inflationary world of 12 and 10, there would be a tremendous onslaught on the social security systems that are in place. Consequently, when we introduced six and five we decided that it had to be applied across the board. I think the results shown in the last six or eight months point to our success in fighting the inflationary psychology that gripped the nation about 14 months ago. In the last three months, we have been successful in bringing the rate of inflation down to the 7.2 per cent range.
In addition, when we introduced the six and five program to our social security system, we reiterated to the House that in order to protect those who need protection most, we would also introduce several countervailing balances in the legislation. In Bill C-132 the Child Tax Credit was increased by $50 in order to protect people on the lower end of the income scale.
The Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) referred to social security and Family Allowances as pork-barrelling. I find that difficult to comprehend, Mr. Speaker.
Some Members of the Opposition have called this Bill an attack on universality. In committee we have pointed out that there are evidently some misconceptions in the minds of Members of the Opposition about what universality is. We have steadfastly maintained throughout debate that there has been no attack on universality in Bill C-131 and Bill C-132. In both instances we have ensured that people at the lower end of the income scale would receive full compensation for our fight against inflation.
The Hon. Member for Western Arctic and others have also said that they would welcome a much wider debate on the whole social security system. We would welcome that as well, Mr. Speaker. The problem is that there never seems to be one spokesman for the Opposition Party who can offer a main platform for that Party. When the Hon. Member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) was Minister of National Health and Welfare in the Conservative Government in 1979, he wanted to dismantle Family Allowances.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes I have I would like to voice my opposition to this closure motion and to give several reasons as to why I feel we should vote against it. It is important to have an opportunity for full and adequate debate in the House of Commons on this particular issue. When we take a look at the entire question of Family Allowances, the underlying principle is that an attack on families is being brought forward at this time by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin). We have had ample indication of the way in which families are being attacked. For example, the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola), in recent press statements, attacked women working in the home. But first I want to take a look at the history of Family Allowances. It is important to keep this aspect in mind. It is always good to have an historical perspective when discussing a contemporary issue. This particular issue bears well in that regard.
It was back in 1945 that Prime Minister Mackenzie King introduced the baby bonus. I suppose it could be underlined that he was a bachelor and childless. It is rather ironic that we have the equivalent of the opposite sex introducing her Bill at this time which attacks that previous positive move. Approximately three years later the baby bonus was made universal. In the early years of the 1970s the Liberal Government attempted to introduce a Bill which would have made the baby bonus selective. Fortunately, after the 1972 election we had a minority Government, and the Liberal Government of the day did not proceed with its plan "to do in" the baby bonus. In fact, during
Time Allocation
that minority Parliament, because of pressure from the Opposition, the then Minister of Health conducted a study and brought in a paper. In 1973 the baby bonus payments were tripled.
The reason I bring forward this historical perspective on a contemporary issue is that it indicates the wisdom which sometimes results if there is opportunity for debate or opportunity for sober second thought. In the early 1970s, in the dying days of Parliament, the Liberal Government wanted to rush through a reduction and elimination of the baby bonus. Then it had second thoughts after the 1972 election. This indicates the wisdom of second thought.
Let me take a look as well at some of the sociological arguments in favour of maintaining Family Allowances as we now know them. When we take a look at Family Allowances, I think we should keep in mind that they are taxable. They are progressive in the sense that the larger one's income, the greater share of one's allowance will be returned to the Government at tax time. The cost of administering the Family Allowance scheme is certainly less expensive than a Child Tax Credit scheme. For example, the administrative costs of Family Allowances from 1976 to 1977 were estimated to be $1.50 per child, or half of 1 per cent in total costs. The estimates for administering alternative schemes such as the Child Tax Credit was something to the tune of ten times those costs.
In addition, there are other reasons we should look positively at the Family Allowance scheme. It is a monthly program. Money is received on a monthly basis, quite often by single parents. Certainly it is easier to budget on a monthly basis than it is to receive a lump sum payment under the Child Tax Credit scheme. Another benefit of a universal Family Allowance scheme is the participation rate. So often, on selective programs such as the Child Tax Credit, many people might not be as aware of it as they should be. They might not be able to fill in the income tax forms as they would like to do. I say this from firsthand experience. As Members of Parliament, we have many people coming to our offices requesting assistance with the Child Tax Credit scheme. There are problems in terms of the incomplete take-up of programs such as the Child Tax Credit. One does not face these problems when there is a universal system such as Family Allowance.
I suppose some people want to argue that the Family Allowance system might be costlier to Government because it can defer the payment of the Child Tax Credit to later in the year. In countering that argument I would want to point out that most income taxes and other taxes are collected earlier in the year. Arguments which attempt to indicate that economically it is better if the Government can hold on to people's money until Child Tax Credit time are certainly not sound ones. It is important to take a look, not only at the historial perspective and some of the sociological considerations, but at the situations in our own constituencies.
In the couple of minutes remaining, I would like to give an indication of what would be the impact on constituencies such

February 7, 1983
Time Allocation
as the riding of Dauphin, Manitoba. It is important to keep in mind that often the Family Allowance program assists the poorer regions of the country. For example, the 1971 statistics indicated that the national household income for families was $9,367. For Manitoba it was $8,261, but for areas such as Dauphin it was $5,361. When one looks at such small household incomes one realizes the impact of the monthly Family Allowance will certainly be much greater than it would be in some of the urban centres. When one reviews the whole question of poverty in Canada, it is important to note that the Family Allowance is most beneficial to single parents and those who are poor in many regions of the country. In Manitoba alone, 63 per cent of the poor adults in that Province are female, many of whom will be affected by Bills such as this. Nearly one-third of the poor are children. It is the children who benefit from these regular monthly Family Allowance payments. Many mothers who have visited my constituency office have told me that they use this Family Allowance to provide such necessities as food, clothing and shelter. This money is made good use of by these families.
One out of every two single-parent families is poor, and many live in ridings such as mine. I think it is important that we oppose the Government's motion to limit debate on a matter as important and crucial as this. I believe that we should have the opportunity to expand on some of the ideas I have mentioned so that Members of the Government will have an opportunity to weigh some of these arguments and perhaps even have an opportunity to examine their own conscience. Moral considerations are involved in this issue as well.
I see that my time has elapsed. I thank you for giving me the opportunity to share some of these concerns. I trust the Members opposite will take them into consideration as we look at this closure motion.

Mr. Speaker, it seems that every time we have one of these debates it is necessary to remind Members opposite of the purpose of the debate. One thing that it is not intended for is to debate the merits of the Bill.
There is a motion before us now which cannot be debated for more than two hours-although we seem to be falling into the practice that the maximum also becomes the minimum- on whether we should allocate and specify how much further time should be spent on this particular Bill. I plan to deal with that motion rather than the merits of the Bill which has been debated over a number of days and will be debated for two more whole days in the House if this motion carries, as I assume it will.
I think it important to remind Hon. Members opposite, since they have not yet realized it, that we are not dealing with closure in this debate. The matter of closure comes under Standing Order 37, and I would invite Members to look it up in their Standing Orders. They will find that closure falls under Standing Order 37, formerly Standing Order 33. We are
dealing here with time allocation under Standing Order 82, formerly Standing Order 75 until the recent rule changes.
I suggest that the public should be made aware of the fundamental difference between these two Standing Orders. If not, I think Members of the Opposition may find themselves becoming somewhat like the boy who cried wolf. They will call time allocation "closure" on so many occasions that in the event there is a real closure motion, no one will think anything of it because they will not know the difference. If a closure motion does occur, I suspect we will then hear speeches about that really being closure as opposed to what they have been calling closure all along.
What is a responsible amount of time to allocate to any debate? This is a problem that any political Party has that is in Government in a parliamentary system. One has to walk a fine line. Parliament is an institution where ideas can be debated. When legislation is introduced, its pros and cons can be thoroughly debated. However, I think we would all concede that unending debate could lead to abuse. In fact, a Government would not be living up to its responsibility to govern if it allowed the legislative flow to become a trickle as a result of spending too much time on debate.
I think it is fair to say that this is one of three Bills which relate to the Government's six and five program. This program was designed to bring inflation under control in this country. It is a statistical fact that it has met with some success to date. While it may be arguable that the amount of progress we have made in reducing inflation in this country being attributable to the Government's six and five program may be argued, I think it is fair to say that the program's psychological impact has been headed in the right direction.
We have been debating the pros and cons of six and five as it relates to other Bills. This is not the only Bill on which six and five will be debated. As has been pointed out by prior speakers, we have discussed this particular Bill before us on December 1, December 2, December 3, in committee and then at report stage on December 17 and December 18. Prior to today there have been over 35 speakers debating this Bill. We are now in a two-hour debate in which we will probably have a total of 12 speakers because of a ten-minute time limit per speaker. We will then have two more full days of debate.
I would suggest that any reasonable, fair-minded and objective person would readily concede that that is a reasonable amount of time to argue the other side of this Bill. 1 dare say that after three or four rounds of speeches, the odds of any new pearls of wisdom or perceptive insights being brought out in debate are rather slim. I really question to what extent the public is served by what really boils down to filibuster and obstruction. Perhaps what is in the minds of some Hon. Members opposite-I certainly do not suggest this of those who are present at the moment-is that some political points can be gained by forcing us to introduce time allocation at each stage of all these Bills. Who can say whether their judgment is right? Only time will tell. Perhaps political futures will be determined on matters other than these.
February 7, 1983

There are times when it is much easier to be in the Opposition than it is to be in Government-probably most of the time. Governments must take decisions that are not necessarily particularly popular. I suppose that everyone wants more rather than less. If one conducts a survey one can probably find people who will say things that are mutually incompatible. How often do I hear from the other side that we should be working for a balanced budget? How often do I hear from the Tories that we should be trying to reduce Government spending. The Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) is sometimes affectionately known as the slasher, and we think of him in those terms in a kindly way. He feels very strongly that Government spends too much. He had a Cabinet post that concerned control of Government expenditures during the previous administration headed by the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark). When he was in office we heard a lot of noise, but when it came down to the specifics about where these cuts would actually come from, he was a little more vague.
It is a little discouraging to be castigated on an almost daily basis for spending too much money when one is trying to take some initiatives which are responsible and which apply equally to everyone in Canada across the board, in a way which does not particularly target out any one group. All of these measures are designed to bring inflation under control, and if we succeed in that, I think that everyone in Canada will be better off in the long run. That is a very desirable thing to do, but when one tries to do it, every possible roadblock is put in one's way. I think it is only fair, in deciding how much time is to be allocated, to ensure that sufficient time has been spent to hear all the arguments. We have long since gone past that stage, and a vote on the Bill at this point would really amount to constructive, responsible and effective leadership on the part of the Government.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO STATUTE LAW
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to add my voice to the chorus of frustrated and angry Canadians who have spoken out against the disaster and regressive measures contained in the last three budgets presented by this Government. On three occasions, November, 1981, June, 1982, and again in October, 1982, this Government has had the chance to bring forward measures which would help stimulate and promote growth in the stagnating economic climate which we know now exists in Canada. Three times, Mr. Speaker, it has failed miserably. The budgets which were presented were a debacle, a "hound's breakfast", if you will. Obviously, the Government itself knew belatedly the mess it had created, knew without reservation it had produced three "clunkers".
