speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, I have all the more respect for you.
Everything this Government does points to state control, including the provisions in this tax Bill. It points to bail-outs for the large corporations, and I am afraid to think about what might happen to Canagrex when it comes back to this House. What will happen will be, of course, closure and, of course, state control. What is next, Mr. Speaker, is it the banks? What is it that will take this country straight into the real and utter debacle of socialism?
The first indication we had that these measures in this Bill were unpalatable and unworkable was when changes and amendments were hastily introduced. It was the second signal from a beleagured Government which gave indication of the serious nature of the problems it had created. The master craftsman, the architect of the first two monstrosities, the then Minister of Finance, was removed from his portfolio, and not before time. Having created havoc within the country, he was given the outside world to tinker with, a threatre of operation where he presumably can do less damage, given the levels of
respect this Government has engendered in international circles, other than an attempt at world socialism. But this shuffle of Ministers did little, if anything, to assure Canadians personally, or the business community in particular, that the economy could be turned around. Does anyone honestly believe for an instant that Canadians now feel safer, now that the Department of Finance is in the hands of the man who was directly responsible for the disastrous National Energy Program? The fire is no worse now than the frying pan was.
The new Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) had the embarrassing task of changing some of the outlandish proposals of his predecessor, but in doing so, he added some objectionable ones of his own. The Bill before us today gives ample proof of this continuing debacle. There were approximately 168 provisions in the original Bill. Due to strong public opposition from the public, and from this Party in particular, some 42 changes have taken place. And the Party to my left had not very much to do with these changes. There were 42 changes, Mr. Speaker, roughly one-quarter of the provisions had to be changed, because this Government never stopped to look before it leaped. Four jumps forward, one jump back for the Canadian economy. In the meantime, confusion and chaos.
Back in December, 1981, I spoke on the Small Businesses Loans act which was directly affecting the budget at that time. I would just like to read from the record because I believe it is very interesting. It is on page 14135 of Hansard for Wednesday, December 16, 1981 and it reads:
This budget is a destroyer of initiative. It is a destroyer of any form of elitism. It is the work of warp-minded bureaucrats who cannot define the meaning of the work risk and who have never met a payroll. I am including the so-called finance minister, unfortunately. Any self-respecting minister of finance in the federal system of government that we know, any self-respecting minister who has had such public opposition of the budget and its contents from the public and from business, any minister who has made such wide-ranging changes in the tax system without consulting small business, any minister who has made a $600 million mistake, any minister who has made three major changes as an admission of error, would and should resign.
Since then, we have had 39 more changes. These changes from November 12 to December 18 include MURBs, reorganizations, reserves, capital cost allowances, soft costs work in progress, restricted interest expenses, retiring allowances, accrual of interest income, IACCs, small business bonds, loans to non-residents and employer housing loans, prescribed rate of interest, DPSPs, life insurance, life insurance policy holders, contractual commitment, airline passes, jet fuel, fiscal arrangements, charitable foundations, federal sales tax, capital cost allowances. All of these have been spoken on at length by my colleagues. Then there have been changes with regard to the automobile standby charge, corporate distribution tax, forward averaging, IACCs, life insurance, all on June 28, 1982. The litany of horrors goes on and on.
As I sat in the House, Mr. Speaker, and heard these three previous budgets, as a small businessman I could not believe the confusion and contradictory nature of the changes and proposals which have had such a serious impact on small

February 7, 1983

business in this country. I would remind the Members opposite that 65 per cent of the businesses in this country are classified as small businesses, and these businesses are the most penalized because of the inept handling of finance by this Government. This is one area which I can speak on from personal experience. Seeing and hearing these proposals-many now rescinded but most still in place-I could almost feel a personal vendetta by the Minister of Finance toward my small business and my employees, not to mention the farmer or the insurance man, etc. Let me illustrate.
Many small-businessmen and farmers, who planned on setting aside funds for their retirement, will suffer as the result of the abolition of the IAACs. The 12.5 per cent dividend distribution tax and the half year convention on capital cost allowances, a subject which has been gone into in great depth here this afternoon, will hurt small-businessmen. Married couples, who now each own a dwelling, usually a home and a cottage, will now be subject to capital gains taxes on one of the residences. The proposed tax liability for directors will discourage individuals from serving on boards of directors. Employees will now be penalized by the inclusion in taxable income of all interest subsidies from an employer, and there will be a deterrent to education through the restriction on education deductions. Employees who have the use of an employer-owned or leased automobile for personal use will now be taxed according to a complicated formula. If I have time, Mr. Speaker, I would like to go into that in great detail.
The Government is penalizing the one thing in this economy of ours which works, that is sales. A person who uses a car on company business will generate sales, which in turn generates production, and that is what we so desperately need in Canada. Canadians will no longer be allowed to deduct interest on loans taken out to purchase registered retirement savings plans. Accrual taxation of life insurance, while watered down from the initial proposal, remains a deterrent to potential purchasers.
In addition to the disastrous effects this Bill will have on the Canadian business community, it raises problems for individual Canadians. The language of the Bill is so complex as to be virtually incomprehensible. It is the most complex piece of legislation since the woebegone days of 1971 when there was supposedly tax reform. I believe Canadians deserve more. They deserve a taxation Act they can know and understand, one which is written in simple style. They do not need an Act which requires the skill of a Philadelphia lawyer to interpret every word and nuance. They do not need tax consultants to explain what it means. Just to give you an idea of what I mean, Mr. Speaker, let me quote from page 58a of the Act as follows:
Clause 20: (1) and (2). The amendment to subparagraph 44(l)(e)(iii) and the new subsection 44(1.1) would implement paragraph (36) of the Income Tax Motion, which is quoted in the note to subclause 12(6).
Subparagraph 44( 1 )(e)(iii) at present reads as follows:
And on and on. That should really make Canadian taxpayers understand what it is all about. In particular, they do not
Income Tax
need two Ministers of Finance in a row going flip-flop in their minds over the tax system, making these 40 some odd changes to date. Of course, those who suffer the most under these regressive measures are low-income Canadians who gain nothing from the lowering of marginal tax rates, and who will lose more proportionately from partial deindexation. The nondeductibility of interest on money borrowed to purchase RRSPs will certainly discourage personal investment. The Government's plan to tax benefits resulting from share purchase loans will reduce the trend toward employee share ownership. Because this Bill will deny registration for future deferred profit-sharing plans which allow an owner, such as myself, to qualify as a beneficiary of the plan, many small, owner-managed firms will not bother instituting such plans, leaving both owners and employees without job related retirement income.
I would like to take a moment, Mr. Speaker, to touch on one of the most important segments not addressed in this budget, the right of Canadians to own property and to have a tax reduction for the ownership of that property. I would like to address this as the blurb on MURB. Among those groups in society which are in drastic need of some direction and assistance from Government are homeowners and home buyers. The Progressive Conservative Government proposed making mortgage interest payments and municipal property taxes a deductible expense from taxable income. This program would have provided a major stimulus to the economy and would have aided thousands of Canadians who have a strong desire to own their own homes. I ask people to think about the fact that that program would have been coming into its final year, and think of what it would have done for those myriads of Canadians who have the ideals I have just stated. At the time the Government scoffed at the idea and rejected this important program out of hand. But what did the Government offer as an alternative? This is the interesting part. On 18 separate occasions in this House-and I have Hansard with me documenting what I am about to say-in the period from November 13, 1980 to November 16, 1981, the then Minister responsible for housing, when queried on the sorry state of housing in Canada and the Government's do-nothing attitude, referred each and every time to MURBs as the magic solution. Hansard makes very interesting reading. Every time we asked him about housing, he stood in his place and said: "MURB, MURB, MURB". Well, where are the MURBs? They have been cancelled, and so has the chance of Canadians for mortgage relief. Where in this Bill, Mr. Speaker, is there any mention of programs which will be of benefit to homeowners or home buyers? Where is the tax relief we had planned to offer? Nowhere.
We were successful, in one of the points I mentioned, in deferring the tax from the wholesale level where the Government wanted to place it, rather than on the manufacturing level where it now rests. When the Minister of Finance could not explain exactly how the measures were even going to be put in place, he said that the change would be 1 per cent or 2

February 7, 1983
Income Tax
per cent to make up the difference from the wholesale level. He said it was completely equitable. He said there would be no increase in the Government's take. Can you think of anything as ridiculous? There is a profit between the manufacturing and wholesale levels, and when you tax the lesser, who is the winner?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO STATUTE LAW
speechtext: The Government.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO STATUTE LAW
speechtext:
Absolutely. These figures 1 am going to quote will give you an idea of what 1 am talking about. Does the Government realize that in addition to the people who are classed as wholesale merchants there are about 5,000 establishments classed as agents and brokers? In 1978, the last reported year, their accumulated gross sales amounted to $16.3 billion. Given the growth over the past ten years it would be safe to assume that today we have between 26,500 and 30,000 wholesale establishments in the country made up of wholesale merchants, agents, brokers, etc. When you add tax at that level, you can understand just what is going to happen to our tax system. More and more will be grabbed by the Government. No respect for the Laffer curve, no respect for what economists in this country are saying about the need for increased productivity and incentives. In 1978, the last year for which we have complete statistics, wholesalers bought $53.9 billion worth of goods, sold those goods for $70.6 billion, and had the tax been in effect then, wholesalers would have had to pay federal sales tax on the difference. Three years ago that difference was approximately $17 billion. Who would have been the winner? Who would have been the loser? The Canadian taxpayer.
Let us look for a moment at that place, as I mentioned before, where everything happens, the point of sale. Nothing in the free world happens until something is sold. It is sold by a salesman, and in today's world this country runs on rubber and petroleum. This salesman must ride in a car. His selling helps the manufacturer increase productivity and, simply put, the circle keeps on widening and we derive taxes. But you cannot keep taxing that poor salesman until there is no incentive left. Often the commissions cannot cover what this Government has done to the salesman who drives the company car.
I would like to read into the record, Mr. Speaker, a letter from the Association of Canadian Travellers which I received. It reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Lalonde:
RE: LEGISLATION PROPOSED-PERSONAL USE BENEFITS OF A COMPANY OWNED VEHICLE
Our Association of 7000 Commercial Travellers feel you should reconsider the proposed Legislation and consider the increases if necessary within the 6% and 5% Guidelines at this time.
It is of great concern that this type of Legislation was placed on all individuals driving employer-owned autos without the advice of Professional Salesmen, "The Commercial Traveller". I am sure your Department Adviser did not research this area.
This Legislation requires study because there should be several degrees of Benefit for the various Salary levels. You could also have asked the families of Commercial Travellers of the Benefits to have a Company Car filled with Advertising, Sales Record Books, Samples, which have to be moved before personal family usage is possible. You might find that Travellers do not go for
Sunday Drives. You might find that many Travellers end up with Medical problems from excessive driving.
A Company Car is worse than your own because the driver personally has to pay the parking lot dents. Most Companies will not allow the Salesman to put on a Trailer Hitch to pull a Holiday Trailer. You cannot add Tape Decks or Air Conditioning with all Firms, as these are luxuries.
The regulations seem to treat everyone regardless of circumstances in the same manner. It is completely ridiculous that a Commercial Traveller should pay in Taxable Benefits, over 3 years, for his working vehicle. A Car is a tool of his trade, like the plumber and his tools.
What would be next-tax the desk in an office because all Canadians don't have one. Tax all Office Workers because they have access to a Photocopier, a Typewriter, or the Postage Meter, etc.
Personal Insurance is high because of theft, i.e. Samples must be taken into the Motel room because some products freeze or would be stolen.
A great many Commercial Travellers that work in the Food, Drug, and Service Areas that have an employer supplied vehicle presently earn less than our Postal Workers. Many of these same Travellers will not even get the 6/5 because of the Economic downturn. Many Travellers are being asked to reduce outside trips, use less expensive Hotels, and are being advised there will be no raises this year at all.
In conclusion, our Association believes that the Standby charge, as proposed is excessive because it is based on the value to employer and not the net Benefit to the employee.
We support the suggestion by our fellow Commercial Travelling Organizations that effective date of this Legislation should be postponed until the 1983 Taxation year.
Yours truly,
A. D. McIntyre.
I most heartily concur with that letter, Mr. Speaker. This tax is not fair and is not imposed equitably. As proof of that let us make some assumptions about the use of a company owned automobile. First, we will assume that the capital cost was $10,000; second that it is company owned; third, that the operation cost is ten cents per kilometer, and fourth, that the cost of operating a standard size car is 18 cents per kilometer. Using the 12,000 kilometer rating that the Government wants to impose, the taxable benefit of the standby charge would be $2,400; operating charges would be $1,200; the cost of operation, taking 12,000 kilometers at 18 cents per kilometer, would be $2,160 and the excess taxation to the travelling salesman, who is producing trade for the country, would be $ 1,440.
When this became evident in my firm, Mr. Speaker, how many salesmen do you think were knocking on my door asking for a raise? It is totally inflationary and is opposed to what we are supposed to be accomplishing.
If we want to use a lesser amount for the standby charge below 12,000 kilometers, we can work with 10,000. In that case, the taxable benefit would be $2,000, operating charges, $1,000, cost of operation for 10,000 kilometers at 18 cents per kilometer, $1,800 and the excess taxation $1,200 or 66.6 per cent. The Bill is repulsive to individual Canadian taxpayers and small-businessmen, Mr. Speaker. I wish it could be withdrawn but I am sure that is a pipedream.
I should like to close by repeating something that I have said many times in this House and outside, Mr. Speaker. You cannot bring about prosperity by discouraging thrift; you
February 7, 1983

cannot strengthen the weak by weakening the strong; you cannot help the wage earner by pulling down the wage payer; you cannot help the poor by destroying the rich; you cannot establish sound security on borrowed money; you cannot keep out of trouble by spending more than you earn; you cannot build character and courage by taking away man's initiative and independence; you cannot help men permanently by doing for them what they could and should do for themselves-and that means without regressive taxation, Mr. Speaker.
The words of Lincoln are as good today as when he wrote them.

subtopic: TRUST COMPANIES-ACTION TAKEN BY MINISTER. (B) QUERY RESPECTING ROLE OF MINISTER
TRUST COMPANIES-ACTION TAKEN BY MINISTER. (B) QUERY RESPECTING ROLE OF MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 26, I had occasion in this House to ask a question of the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove) regarding the affairs of Greymac, Seaway Trust and the other companies that are now under receivership or seizure by officers of the Government of Ontario.
The whole problem in relation to these trust companies has been expressed by Hon. Members on this side and, indeed, the general public. It is of major concern to the Province of

February 7, 1983
Adjournment Debate
Ontario right now. It has been bothering the House of Commons and its Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs for a number of months, indeed, years.
The Government is responsible under the Constitution for banks, banking, money supply, interest rates and the various powers which go along with the creation and management of money. Consequently we have several organs of Government which are supposed to be responsible to be our policemen and to manage these affairs. We have a Trust Companies Act and a Loan Companies Act and a director. We have the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation which insures deposits to $20,000, and hopefully that will soon be $60,000 to protect those who deposit in loan and trust companies, banks and so on. We have an Inspector General of Banks. In addition, we have the actions of the Bank of Canada and the efforts which are supposed to be made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and his Department. All these actions are supposed to ensure for the people of Canada that our financial system is sound and secure.
Unfortunately there have been real stirrings, particularly in this session of Parliament, with respect to these financial institutions. The House will recall that earlier this year following a motion there was a special reference to the Finance Committee with respect to banks and bank profits. Very soon that Committee became a bank solvency committee, not a bank profit committee. In accordance with its deliberations, the Committee made reference to increasing deposit insurance to $60,000 and other recommendations to Government, all with the view to increasing the security of our financial system.
The House will also recall that when the Bank Act was before it, the former minister of state for finance gave solid undertakings, both in the House and in Committee, that he would introduce new loan and trust company provisions before the House. All we have had is a White Paper on the trust company matter, but no new statute or proposal from Government.
This matter has become quite serious. Seaway and Greymac are both federal corporations with respect to their mortgage operations. They were incorporated during the life of this Parliament. They are now in trouble. The Government has known of some of the problems for over a year. The Government has known that the officers behind Greymac in particular were involved in trying to get control of the Canadian Commercial Bank. There have been concerns expressed to the Government on the problems of Astra Trust and ReMor. The Government knows of the problems of Argosy. Prior to all this there were problems with British Mortgage and Trust and Atlantic Acceptance.
The whole question of the stability of our financial institutions is at stake. Every day that goes by with the Government stonewalling questions in the House concerning Seaway and Greymac, what it is doing and where it stands, causes further concern to depositors and others who want to deal with trust companies, loan companies and banks. In the view of this fact, the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Bill now before the House should be expedited. Because it cannot be expedited unless the Government undertakes that this House will have a
complete inquiry by a special committee into the activities of loans and trust companies generally, and into the activities of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation and the Inspector General of Banks particularly, I say to you and the House, it is absolutely essential that the Government take its responsibilities seriously and deal very quickly with new methods of regulating and controlling those who have the right to take deposits from the public, make mortgage loans and generally operate our financial system as financial intermediaries. The whole question of our system of finance is at stake. The Government has been hiding. We have had sleeping policemen on the job. There are problems and it is time for the Government to do something about them.

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas Fisher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: TRUST COMPANIES-ACTION TAKEN BY MINISTER. (B) QUERY RESPECTING ROLE OF MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, because Crown Trust Company, Greymac Trust Company and Seaway Trust Company are provincially incorporated, the federal Department of Insurance has no jurisdiction over their activities. Greymac Mortgage and Seaway Mortgage are federally incorporated mortgage loan companies licensed under the Loan Companies Act and supervised by the federal Department of Insurance. The activities of Greymac Mortgage and Seaway Mortgage have been monitored by the Department.
The Loan Companies Act stipulates that the licence of each mortage loan company shall expire on March 31 of each year and may be renewed from year to year, subject to any qualification or limitation that the Minister considers expedient. The Act also stipulates that the licence may be renewed for any term less than a year.
I can report that since March 31, 1982, for a number of reasons, the licences of Greymac Mortgage and Seaway Mortgage have only been renewed for successive periods not exceeding two months. I can also report that as early as April in the case of Greymac Mortgage and July in the case of Seaway Mortgage, limitations were placed in their licences aimed at severely limiting any significant growth in the amount of money the companies could accept from the public. Subsequent to that time, further limitations were placed on the companies' licences and additional action was taken to protect the position of their bond and debenture holders.
On January 7, 1983, the Superintendent took control of the companies' assets, pursuant to Section 73 of the Loans Companies Act, and reported to the Minister, pursuant to Section 73.1 of that act, that in his opinion the companies' assets were not sufficient, having regard to all circumstances, to give adequate protection to their bond and debenture holders. Before the Minister may take any action in respect of this report he must give the companies an opportunity to be heard; that process is now in progress.
Concerning the provincially incorporated Crown Trust, Greymac Trust and Seaway Trust, and the reason why the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation has agreed, if necessary, to lend them funds on a secured basis to meet their
February 7, 1983

liquidity needs, all three companies are members of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. One of the powers of the Corporation is to lend member institutions funds to help them meet their liquidity needs. In addition, because the three trust companies are member institutions, the CDIC stands ready to meet its insurance commitments to the companies' insured depositors, should that be necessary.

subtopic: NORTH ATLANTIC TREATY ORGANIZATION-CANADIAN NAVAL CONTRIBUTION. (B) MODERNIZATION OF VESSELS
NORTH ATLANTIC TREATY ORGANIZATION-CANADIAN NAVAL CONTRIBUTION. (B) MODERNIZATION OF VESSELS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise this evening in reference to a question I asked of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne) on January 31, concerning the status of our destroyers and the DELEX Program. I pointed out during my question that the Canadian Navy is unable to participate fully in NATO exercises because of the unsuitability and age of the equipment. I am concerned tonight with my supplementary question which was:
Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the same Minister. We are spending over $200 million on a destroyer life extension project, as he knows, to extend the life of 16 ancient destroyers.
Gatineau has just come out of the DELEX Program, a 24 year old vessel having its life extended another eight years. It does not provide for, nor has it had installed any form of anti-missile capability. The lessons of the Falklands point to the necessity of that. These ships will not be able to defend themselves in the event of hostilities. Will the Minister tell us why they are only doing half the job of modernizing those vessels?
In answer, the Minister of National Defence stated:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member should know that behind the policy of the DELEX Program, which is a program to modernize our vessels, we are cognizant of the time that we will in fact be able to use these vessels. For the old class of 56 and 57, for example, we will refit them so that they can be used for another seven or eight years, until the new frigates are in service. There is no use spending millions of dollars on something that we will not be able to use in five or six years. However, on the newer class frigates there will be a more complex DELEX Program so that they will be useful for a longer period of time. It is just a question of judgment.
It is not the confusion of the answer that bothers me as much as the fact that, for a considerable length of time yet to come, we will be unable to have any naval vessels which can defend themselves in conventional, non-nuclear war. In the case of a non-nuclear war, Canada would be assigned two major roles; the anti-submarine warfare role and protection and reinforcement convoys. Any future war is likely to be over quickly enough that it will be a "come as you are" war. We will not have time to build ships after the war starts. The Falklands conflict gave military and political leaders some insight as to what can happen, and we should have learned some lessons from it.
Let us consider what the naval forces in the Western world are likely to confront in any future war. I would like to illustrate part of the Soviet capacity of surface ships and submarines. Concerning Cruise missile carriers, there are 50 Cruise-missile-carrying nuclear powered submarines in the Russian fleet at the present time. There are 20 Cruise-missile-carrying diesel-electric powered submarines in its fleet. The Soviets have just deployed a new KIROV class destroyer which carries 20 long range, or 500 kilometre range, Cruise missiles. In
Adjournment Debate
addition, there are 26 guided missile cruisers, 38 guided missile destroyers, and 28 guided missile frigates in the fleet.
The largest Soviet surface ship is the Kiev-class aircraft carrier. Two have been deployed and two more are under construction. The Kievs are armed with anti-ship Cruise missiles, anti-submarine and over-the-horizon target acquisition helicopters, anti-aircraft missiles, anti-submarine rockets and missiles, and the FORGER vertical and short-takeoff-and landing aircraft.
The common factor in recent Soviet naval developments is increasing size. Larger than their predecessors, these new ships and submarines have larger weapon magazines and greater endurance. The Soviet Naval Air Force has been receiving the supersonic swing-wing backfire bomber, which is equipped with AS-6 anti-ship missiles. That missile has a range of more than 200 kilometres. To complement the anti-ship missiles, the Soviet Union has developed and deployed two types of low-orbiting satellites for global ocean surveillance.
Having regard to ship defence, what must any modern fleet need? It needs patrol aircraft for reconnaissance. It would also be well advised to have the Airborne Warning and Control System Aircraft. This is one of the things Britain found itself desperately short of during the Falklands war. A fleet must have long range air defence missiles to attack enemy launching platforms, anti-submarine weapons such as ASROC, which is a Mark 46 torpedo on an unguided rocket, and uses a homing device to find submarines to a depth of 11 kilometres, modern depth charge launchers and ASW helicopters. A fleet needs short range point defence, such as anti-missile missiles to shoot down attacking missiles, or a sophisticated electronic countermeasures system to jam the missiles' guidance system, or a chaff dispenser. We have none of these. It also needs close in automatic gun systems.
What does Canada have? We have 23 destroyers, of which three are not operational, and only four of the remaining 20 are modern. By the time the six new patrol frigates have all been delivered, in 1991, Canada will have a ten ship navy.
The youngest ship, apart from the DDH-280s, will be an Annapolis class, which was produced in 1964. The DDH-280 has been fitted with the Sea Sparrow system which, as Commodore Healey told the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, has a very limited capability against second generation missiles. I notice that an advertisement for the Sea Sparrow states, "The Sea Sparrow has successfully intercepted missiles as well as Cruise missile type targets and has proved its ECCM capabilities". I must say that there is a certain amount of puffery in that advertisement, because the type of missiles that they can intercept are not the Exocet. In fact, Canada has no protection for its ships against the Exocet or any other sea skimming missile.
Canada's contribution to the Supreme Allied Command Atlantic this year will be the 26-year old HMCS Margaree, which has no missiles and 1960s technology. The Destroyer Life Extension Program relates to 16 destroyers. First will be the St. Laurent class which has six vessels, 27 years of age at

February 7, 1983
Adjournment Debate
the present time. They will not get any new equipment but the hull and machinery repairs will keep them safe. The MacKenzie class has four vessels, 21 years of age. The improved Restigouche class has four vessels, 25 years of age and the Annapolis class has two vessels, only 19 years of age, and they are going to treat them the same as the improved Restigouche.
Just in closing 1 might say that the Deputy Minister of Defence at that time, on May 18, 1982 said:
The DELEX will not be fitted with a missile-to-missile capability ... Their main capability is still in the anti-submarine role. If you ended up in a surface-to-surface action where they could run into that type of missile, they would be in very great difficulty.
1 look forward to whatever the Parliamentary Secretary can say that might comfort me in this matter.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Hudecki (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NORTH ATLANTIC TREATY ORGANIZATION-CANADIAN NAVAL CONTRIBUTION. (B) MODERNIZATION OF VESSELS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will first of all touch on the DELEX program. Quite frankly, it is rather surprising to hear the Hon. Member's concerns in this regard. The Hon. Member knows that the DELEX program was in the departmental approval process between 1977 and 1980 and in fact received Treasury Board's final approval in January 1980 when the Hon. Member was Minister of National Defence. 1 wonder if it has escaped the Hon. Member's notice that it was he who approved the DELEX program.
From the outset, the DELEX program was constrained in order to accommodate the expenditure within the DND envelope; while still permitting the continued allocation of funds for new equipment; such as the Canadian patrol frigate.
While the total cost of the DELEX program, when completed, will be in the area of $200 million, I think it is important to point out that these funds will be spread over 16 ships. The funds were assigned as follows: all 16 ships, regardless of age, went through a thorough refit, thus ensuring that they could safely proceed to sea for some additional years beyond their projected retirement date. Approximately $80 million of DELEX funds were allocated to this expenditure. The remaining funds were assigned to ships in order to maintain a combat capability for their remaining life, and were assigned to individual ships on the basis of how much longer we anticipate that they would have to remain in service before new ships could replace them.
In this division, or allocation of combat capability funds, the St. Laurent class, our oldest ships, received nothing. The MacKenzie class received approximately $7 million per ship; the improved Restigouche class received approximately $17 million per ship and the Annapolis class, our newest steam destroyers, received approximately $19 million each.
It is true that none of these older ships received an antimissile missile system. The funds available were simply not sufficient to make major changes in old ships and preserve capital for the real requirement of acquiring new ships. However, in time of imminent conflict, such changes can be incorporated into our active fleet.
However, in dealing with these newer ships we have made several high technology improvements. In the case of Gatineau and the improved Restigouche class, it has already received most of the new DELEX equipment and will receive the remainder when it is available from the production lines. These include: (a) improved secure communications; (b) improved air warning radar; (c) upgraded gun/fire control system; (d) improved electronic warfare system; (e) a new missile decoy system; (f) a nev' automated link and plotting system and (g) an improved Identification Friend or Foe system. Similar improvements will fitted in the other improved Restigouche and Annapolis classes.

subtopic: GARRISON DIVERSION-RESTORATION OF UNITED STATES FUNDING-REQUEST THAT MINISTER TAKE ACTION. (B) REPORTED STATEMENTS MADE BY NORTH DAKOTA OFFICIAL
GARRISON DIVERSION-RESTORATION OF UNITED STATES FUNDING-REQUEST THAT MINISTER TAKE ACTION. (B) REPORTED STATEMENTS MADE BY NORTH DAKOTA OFFICIAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was most distressed over the $22.33 million recently allocated by the United States Government for the continuing construction of the Garrison Diversion Project. However, I was extremely perturbed when I learned that the United States House-Senate Conference Committee had been persuaded to reinstate $4 million of funding for Garrison, originally voted against in the United States House of Representatives.
The very first legislative setback in the project's history occurred in mid-December when Congress denied the allocation of $4 million to the detrimental project. This was the only glimmer of hope for Canada's environmental welfare seen in the 18-year history of Garrison. Finally, it was felt by some, Canada had made headway in the battle to convince the United States that the irrigation project would be harmful to our waterways and Manitoba's fishing and agricultural industries.
One week later, however, the moneys were restored. As reported in the January 3, 1983 Time Magazine, Congressman Silvio Conte publicly stated in Washington that the driving force behind the completion of Garrison, North Dakota's Senator Mark Andrews urged the House-Senate Conference Committee to reinstate funding for Garrison or risk having him vote against their pet projects.
To toy with such matters of importance to Canada is, I feel, a disgrace. Whether the United States House-Senate Conference Committee decided to vote for or against the proposed funding is not the issue here. The fact is the seriousness of the Garrison Diversion Project and, in particular, that the proven harmful effects it will have are not being taken into consideration. Furthermore, for Senators to base the logic of their vote on the criterion of ensuring the life of their own pet projects is totally ludicrous.
For 18 years Canadians have been expressing their objections to the continuation of this project. It is a known fact that
February 7, 1983

if Garrison is completed, Canadian waters will be contaminated, causing Manitoba's industries to suffer. The project will result in a violation of the 1909 Boundary Waters Treaty between Canada and the United States, thereby totally disregarding the affirmation of the International Joint Commission. All evidence compiled on the project points to the disastrous consequences it would have on our country.
The facts have been presented time and time again. 1 have recommended to this Elouse on numerous occasions the need to make representation to the United States Government, airing our valid concern and objection to the completion of the project. I have been in contact with the Ambassador of the United States, His Excellency Paul H. Robinson, Jr., obtaining his assurances that in no way would the United States violate its obligation to the Boundary Waters Treaty or ignore the recommendations of the International Joint Commission.
Still there are those resolved to completing the project with utter indifference to the outcome for Canada. In The Globe and Mail of November 25, 1982, Robert Wefald, the Attorney General for North Dakota stated, and I quote:
The bottom line is the project will be built if the United States Government decides it is in our best interests.
However, according to Congressman Conte and the Joint House-Senate Conference Committee, the best interests of a country are irrelevant. It is the better interests of individual Senators' pet projects which are of prime importance and which, as proven with the restoration of funds for Garrison, come first. For this reason I feel it imperative to call upon this House and ask that immediate steps be taken to ascertain the manner in which this inane situation be dealt with.
On June 9, 1982, an all-Party Committee of the House of Commons travelled to Washington and voiced the concern of the Canadian people. It has been made obvious that again we must show our opposition to this project. I agree wholeheartedly with the recommendation of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta), that this House instruct its Ministers and give an indication to the Province of Manitoba to have a committee present itself to Washington to put up a strong showing against funding for Garrison. I must stress the need for speed due to the announced $22.33 million more now allocated to the detrimental Garrison Diversion Project.
Mr. Jean Lapierre (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs).
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for his keen interest in the Garrison Diversion Unit Project. I would like to reassure him that this Government has more confidence in the political system of the United States than to think that, as he puts it, an individual Senator's pet project could be a base or a criterion for them to approve the project of such magnitude.
Adjournment Debate
If I may give some history, Mr. Speaker, I would say that the Garrison Diversion Unit, first authorized in 1965 by the U.S. Congress, continues to be a subject of serious concern to the federal Government, as well as to the provincial Government of Manitoba. No one on either side of the Canada-U.S. border contests the fact that if the unit is built to full size it, "would cause severe and irreversible damage to the Manitoba ecosystem and, in particular, to the commercial and sport fisheries in Canada,". This quotation is taken from the 1977 International Joint Commission Report on Garrison, which concluded that, "those portions of the Garrison Diversion Unit which could affect waters flowing into Canada not be built at this time".
The IJC Report, and this conclusion, form the foundation for Canadian opposition to the Garrison Project. We firmly believe, and have so informed the U.S. Government and Congress, that Canadian and Manitoba interests can only be protected through modifications of the project, so that there are no transfers of water from the Missouri River basin into waters of the Hudson Bay basin which flow into Canada.
U.S. authorities have recognized the validity of our position and have formally stated, as has the Ambassador to the Hon. Member, that the United States will comply with its legal obligations to Canada under the 1909 Boundary Waters Treaty not to pollute Canadian waters. Thus, we should not attach much weight to statements by U.S. State officials such as those attributed recently to the Attorney General of North Dakota, or even the Senator from North Dakota, that the Garrison Project will be proceeded with regardless of Canadian or IJC views.
As Hon. Members know, the Congress appropriated $4 million for the project for the fiscal year 1983, despite an initial rejection of this funding by the U.S. House of Representatives. The level of funding proposed for the fiscal year 1984 by the administration is $22 million. While this is a very large increase in the appropriation level, it still must be accepted by Congress. Given the initial defeat of the 1983 appropriation, it is quite possible that Congress will reduce drastically or eliminate an appropriation of this magnitude.
Opposition to the Garrison Project as currently designed is on the increase. We believe that this opposition will influence the administration and Congress to be more forthcoming in finding ways to meet domestic U.S. and Canadian concerns with the design of the project. We will follow up all reasonable means to achieve this goal. We thank the Hon. Member for his continuing support.
